Week 3 is underway, and we're tracking all the injuries heading into the weekend.

Live injury updates

The Seattle Seahawks will have their No. 1 quarterback on Sunday when they take on the Washington Commanders. Sam Darnold, who suffered a glute injury during the opening game of the season, was back at practice on Thursday as a full participant, and was off the injury report on Friday.

In Darnold's absence, Drew Lock threw for 187 yards and a touchdown during Seattle's Week 1 win over the New England Patriots. He followed that up during last week's win over the Arizona Cardinals with 235 passing yards and three touchdowns.

Head coach Mike Macdonald had said Darnold is "on a good track right now" to play in Week 3; on Friday, he said that Darnold is "ready to go."

It's not looking good for Caleb Williams to be available for the Chicago Bears when they play the Philadelphia Eagles on Monday night. The quarterback left Week 2 with a hamstring injury and, according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, is not expected to be available. That would mean the next man up is Tyson Bagent, but he suffered a concussion in practice this week, which could lead to Case Keenum being under center.

Other Week 3 injuries to monitor:

  • Saquon Barkley suffered a stinger in Week 2, but after positive MRI results he returned to practice with the Eagles on Thursday. The team did not list him on their injury report as he was a full participant on Friday.

  • The Washington Commanders and Jayden Daniels got good news with the quarterback not requiring surgery on his injured elbow. General manager Adam Peters said Friday that an operation is "not on the table" and that they have not talked about placing Daniels on injured reserve, which would rule him out for at least four weeks.

  • Nico Collins has been ruled out by the Houston Texans as he deals with a Grade 1 hamstring strain. Like Collins, Zay Flowers of the Baltimore Ravens also missed Week 2 and remained out of practice this week. He is listed as questionable for their game in Brazil.

  • Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua sat out Friday's practice and is doubtful for Sunday night. Head coach Sean McVay said this week Nacua was "not making great progress" with the hip/groin issue that kept him out of Week 2. McVay added they expect Nacua to be ready to return next week.

  • After being ruled out for the season with a knee injury, New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart will undergo surgery on Friday to repair his meniscus. According to The Athletic's Dan Duggan, Dart also suffered damage to his MCL and PCL, which will be addressed if needed. He is looking at a four-to-six month recovery period.

item.title: Reacts Survey Results: Jacksonville’s pass rush is still a problem
item.description: The Jaguars can’t get home with four pass rushers. Who could’ve guessed?!
item.content:encoded:
This week, we asked Jacksonville Jaguars fans to pinpoint the team’s biggest weakness against top teams.

Nearly half of respondents said the pass rush.

Since last year’s Week 8 bye, the Jags are 10-2 in the regular season — but they split two games against the Broncos and lost to the Texans, as well as to the Bills in the playoffs. Their wins in that span came against the Colts (2x), Titans (2x), Jets, Cardinals, Raiders, and Chargers.

Long story short, Liam Coen’s team is still has to prove that they can beat the best teams in the NFL. On a consistent basis.

It would certainly help to have a pass rush that doesn’t rank bottom-10 in pressure rate and total sacks every dang season! The most frustrating part about Jacksonville’s inability to affect opposing passers is that it’s a problem we all saw coming. For crying out loud, find a solution past Ruke Orhororo and Wesley Williams, Gladstone.

As for the confidence survey, 84% of fans are confident the team is headed in the right direction.

According to FanDuel Sportsbook, Jacksonville’s odds to win Super Bowl LXI shifted from +3000 before the season to +2200 after the Week 1 win over Cleveland, and to +2500 after the Week 2 loss in Denver.

There’s a real chance that after this weekend, the Jaguars will be 3-0 and the rest of the AFC South will be 0-9. What a wonderful world that would be.

item.title: Cardinals Kei’Trel Clark fined for using eye black message
item.description: Strict uniform rules must be followed
item.content:encoded:
Arizona Cardinals cornerback Kei’Trel Clark was fined $6,651 for wearing eye black with a message inscribed after last week’s 31-7 loss to the Seattle Seahawks.

The NFL does not play with uniforms. There are a ton of rules and regulations regarding cleats, sweatbands, undershirts, helmets, and the uniform itself.

RELATED:CARDINALS PLACE WILL JOHNSON ON IR

Clark’s message stated:

“GLORY BE (peace symbol) 2 GOD.”

The NFL takes a lot of pride in keeping the presentation of its league professional and clean. If Clark writes in paint pen on his eye black a message, then somebody else takes that cue and writes their own message. Then it is writing on socks or sweatbands, unauthorized logos, paint pen on a cleat, or the tail of a T-shirt hanging.

“Happy Birthday, Tashaun!” would become a weekly message seen on national TV.

Another reason the NFL is so determined is its sponsorships. Uniform makers pay quite a bit to display their logo. Oakley does as well. The NFL doesn’t want painted messages on cleats stating, “Shoe Palace has great deals!” The league does not make any money off of these types of messages, so they outlaw everything.

Clark went to his Instagram account and stated:

“I need answers. 6.6K for giving God the Glory.”

No, 6.6K for not following the league’s uniform code. The NFL does not care about a sack of dried butter beans that you want to promote your faith. Clark has from Monday until Saturday to preach to as many folks as possible about finding God and praising Jesus. But Clark will need to do this within his own space. And it’s not like Clark is a superstar on the Cardinals roster. He currently backs up Denzel Burke at the left cornerback spot.

The specific financial terms and dollar amounts that Oakley pays the NFL are not publicly disclosed, which means it must be pretty lucrative. And all 32 NFL teams get a slice of that deal. The current contract was extended until 2030.

Those are messages on NFL uniforms that pay handsomely.

Eye black today is no longer a traditional roll-on stick. They are like fabric Band-Aids that peel off with glue underneath. They can be written on with silver paint pens very easily before being installed. While playing for the University of Florida, QB Tim Tebow always had a scripture written on his eye black that was seen by millions every game. But once he suited up in the NFL, the written messages ceased.

And it is not like fining Clark is a one-off. The NFL has been consistent about this for years: No writing of any kind on face prints. 

What is odd are the circumstances. At every NFL game, there are uniform cops, called NFL uniform inspectors, on each sideline. They patrol the field during pre-game warmups and remain on the sidelines throughout the entire game, switching sidelines at the end of each quarter to monitor both teams fairly. They are paid by the league instead of through the Cardinals, which makes them act as neutral, league-appointed officials representing the NFL Compliance Department.

They are usually two former players of the team itself. If the inspectors see any discrepancy, they will approach the player and tell them what is wrong, then expect the athlete to correct the situation and are usually cool about the infraction, giving ample time to fix the issue. If the player persists, the uniform cops write it up and submit it to the league.

Players are paid via direct deposit every two weeks. Clark’s deposit will simply be short by $6,651. The second offense of the standard uniform code is $17,911. A third offense can result in game suspensions, for which the player does not get paid whatsoever for each game he is out. The source of the fine is included in Rule 5, Section 4, Article 8 of the NFL’s 2026 rulebook. It states that Clark cited the unauthorized personal message on his eye black regardless of what the message was. 

LINK: LIST OF NFL FINES

Clark seems to be in attack mode ever since he received his fine letter in the mail. He followed it with a string of memes aimed at the fine and also shared a picture of himself wearing eye black marked “INSHALLAH.”

He stated:

“I got to report to God at the end of my days on the day of judgment!” I’ll always give God the glory out loud 😎 All good.”

That is perfectly fine and good. But the league does not care for one minute whether Clark plays in their league or not. His cap hit this year is $1.2 million. Maybe he can get his real estate license and make that kind of money.

This is not Clark’s first run-in with the NFL’s uniform rules. In October 2025, he was fined $5,797 after wearing what the league described as a “black streamer towel” during Arizona’s game against the Indianapolis Colts. Only white licensed towels are approved.  

So, bow up all you want, Clark. It’s your money to lose, and you aren’t going to buck the league rules. You want answers? It is pretty simple: Don’t write on your eye black. Period. Or you will find work as a substitute school teacher in your future very soon.

item.title: Broncos vs. Rams: 3 Players to Watch in Week 3
item.description: These three players need to perform at a high level to help defeat the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday Night Football.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos host the Los Angeles Rams for their Week 3 gridiron matchup in primetime on Sunday Night Football. In order for the Broncos to achieve their second victory of the season, these are three players need to stand out in a big way tomorrow evening.

Zach Allen — Defensive Lineman

It was a night and day difference for the Broncos’ defense when comparing their execution in Week 1 versus Week 2. One player who really stood out to me in their comeback win over the Jaguars was defensive lineman Zach Allen.

Allen may have not been a monster on the traditional stat sheet, but he was consistently applying pressure on Trevor Lawrence all game long. He made their interior offensive line look bad (especially rookie left guard Emmanuel Pregnon) and was a key reason Lawrence had a poor performance through the air.

The eighth-year pro has been a tremendous player for the franchise since coming over alongside Vance Joseph from the Arizona Cardinals in 2023. There’s no doubt he is one of Denver’s best players, and certainly one of the most underrated defensive linemen in the National Football League.

In order to slow down Matthew Stafford and aerial attack of the Rams, Allen’s pass rushing prowess will have to be on display. Over the past few seasons, Los Angeles has done a good job protecting Stafford and giving him plenty of time to hit his array of weapons from the pocket. I’m optimistic Allen will rise to the occasion and cause issues on Sunday night.

Riley Moss — Cornerback

The secondary performed well last Sunday against the Jaguars. Outside of a few busted plays, their coverage was sound and their starting trio at cornerback did an incredible job limiting Trevor Lawrence’s impact through the air. I felt all of them had some great plays throughout the game.

After a few bad plays in Week 1, cornerback Riley Moss came back with a vengeance. His second half interception was a crucial play in the game. It served as a big momentum shift that helped earn the Broncos their first win of the season.

The Rams boast two great receivers in Davante Adams and Puka Nacua. Though it does seem unlikely that Nacua is going to play due to injury. Regardless, I do expect there to be situations where Moss has to go up against Adams—unless the Broncos opt for a defensive gameplan that permanently fixates Patrick Surtain II on him.

Either way, I expect Moss to be targeted often. This offseason, Moss discussed the importance of getting stronger and being more physical at the catch point going up against big receivers. He’ll certainly have an opportunity to do that in primetime. The Broncos will need him to be at his best to keep the Rams’ passing attack from taking off at Mile High.

Luke Wattenberg — Center

The Broncos’ offensive line faces another big test this going up against defensive front seven of the Rams. They have a handful of quality players that have to be kept in check. Denver’s big men up front are going to have to do well to protect Bo Nix. Additionally, they will need block well to jumpstart their running game to have a shot at winning.

Through two games, I think there is certainly improvement to be had from Denver’s offensive line unit. Routinely ranked as one of the NFL’s best heading into the season, they haven’t been firing on all cylinders thus far. One particular offensive lineman that I will be keeping a close eye on is center Luke Wattenberg.

Wattenberg has struggled with some of his snaps this season. He has also been susceptible to giving up interior pressure and dealing with blitzes and stunts. There will be times Aaron Donald is likely isolated on him in one-on-one matchups. Despite coming out of retirement and not playing for several years, Donald had nearly a 28-percent pass rush win rate against the New York Giants.

The fifth-year center is going to need to perform well on Sunday Night Football to keep the future Hall of Famer in check. Denver can’t afford to get beat up the middle if they want to let Nix step up into the pocket and rip it and establish their running attack.

item.title: Cowboys vs. Ravens: Matchups to watch in Week 3
item.description: Where do you think the Cowboys/Ravens game will be won and lost?
item.content:encoded:
Both the Dallas Cowboys and Baltimore Ravens hit the road this week, traveling all the way to Brazil for this Week 3 matchup. Although they are thousand miles from home, this is technically a home game for America’s Team, but we shouldn’t expect any kind of home field advantage. It could be quite the opposite with questionable field conditions.

Anyway you want to look at a this is a tough matchup for the Cowboys. The Ravens are one of the better teams in the league despite losing to the Saints a week ago. This is a game chock-full of matchups that could sway the outcome of the game one way or another. Below we discuss which ones we will be watching closely.

Cowboys’ run defense vs. Ravens’ rushing attack

The Cowboys made an effort to improve their run defense this offseason by bringing in Christian Parker and outside players to help, but as of yet there hasn’t been any sign things have changed. In fact, they are still currently one of the worst against the run in the league, allowing 173.5 yards per game, ranking 30th in the league. That doesn’t exactly inspire much confidence they’ll be able to contain Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry this week. They both headline the fifth-ranked rushing attack so far this year and are averaging 83.5 rushing yards per game.

WR CeeDee Lamb vs. Ravens’ CBs

CeeDee Lamb is coming off a huge game last week against the Commanders and will certainly demand attention from the Ravens cornerbacks in this Week 3 matchup. The last time these two teams played No. 88 had just four catches for 67 yards with no touchdowns and a fumble. This time around Baltimore can’t focus the majority of their attention on him though with George Pickens having to be factored in. Moving Lamb around could create favorable matchups for him or provide one-on-one opportunities for Pickens. It could be a win-win.

Cowboys’ pass rush vs. Ravens’ OL

This is a matchup that could heavily favor the Cowboys considering the Ravens OL is currently allowing a 44% pressure rate through the first two weeks, ranking third-worst in the NFL. The interior of their OL is particularly vulnerable after letting All-Pro C Tyler Linderbaum walk in free agency. Neither Kenny Clark or Quinnen Williams have played up to their typical standards so far, but could both excel in this matchup. And, Donovan Ezeiruaku and Malachi Lawrence could find some success as tackle Ronnie Stanley will be out.

item.title: Previewing the New York Jets’ opposition: Detroit Lions
item.description: The Jets aim for a road win against a tough Detroit Lions opponent
item.content:encoded:
The New York Jets and Detroit Lions are both 1-1 heading into Sunday’s matchup, but both are in search of a bounceback game after the Jets lost in overtime and the Lions gave up 41 points in last Thursday night’s loss to the Bills.

Let’s break down the Lions’ roster going position by position:

Quarterbacks

Jared Goff has had three seasons in a row with over 4,500 passing yards and he’s off to a good statistical start so far in 2026. He leads the league with six touchdown passes and doesn’t have an interception. He has been sacked five times and fumbled three times, though.

Goff has also been durable. This will be his 72nd consecutive start, dating all the way back to the end of the 2021 season.

The Lions moved fast to address their backup situation when Teddy Bridgewater retired in the offseason. His replacement, Josh Dobbs, is an extremely smart quarterback who has started 15 NFL games.

Offensive Line

The Lions had a trio of starting offensive linemen who were limited in practice this week: Left guard Christian Mahogany, right guard Tate Ratledge and right tackle Blake Miller. However, all three returned to practice on Friday and are expected to start.

Mahogany’s return is just in time because Ben Bartch, who started the first two games in his place, is out of this weekend’s game due to injury. He had been struggling in pass protection, so this should be an upgrade, although Mahogany gave up a team-high six sacks in 2025.

The first round rookie Miller will make his return after Larry Borom filled in for him last week. He gave up two sacks and had three penalties, so this again looks like it will be an upgrade.

Left tackle Penei Sewell is their best lineman, having been to the past four pro bowls. He gave up just two sacks last year.

The other starter is Juice Scruggs who is the center, although Cade Mays would probably be starting if he wasn’t on injured reserve. He lines up alongside Ratledge, who led the team in offensive penalties last year.

The other backup is guard Miles Frazier, who was a fifth round pick last year. They will also need to elevate another one with Bartch ruled out.

Running Backs

The two-headed monster is no more, as David Montgomery is now in Houston, but this has freed up Jahmyr Gibbs to try and establish himself as the league’s best running back. He’s off to a decent start with 299 yards from scrimmage in the first two games.

With new addition Isiah Pacheco on injured reserve, the number two is the converted safety Sione Vaki, although he has only 10 carries in three seasons.

Jacob Saylors is the number three, but mostly on the team for his special teams abilities.

Pass catchers

Pro bowler Amon-Ra St. Brown is off to an excellent start this year. He leads the NFL with 19 catches and four touchdown receptions.

He’s by no means the Lions’ only weapon, though, as Jameson Williams is also coming off back-to-back thousand-yard seasons.

Then you have tight end Sam LaPorta, who had 17 touchdowns in his first two seasons before missing eight games last year.

Detroit’s other starting receiver, Isaac TeSlaa, only caught 16 passes last year but six of them were touchdowns and he’s established himself as a big play threat and capable of highlight reel grabs.

Tay Martin and Tom Kennedy are also both on the team at wide receiver but neither has played an offensive snap so far this season.

Depth at tight end comes from ex-Jet Tyler Conklin, Jackson Meeks and Brock Wright. Wright, who also plays fullback, caught a crucial touchdown pass when the 2022 Jets blew a late lead to the Lions in the last meeting between these teams.

Defensive Line

Former number two overall pick Aidan Hutchinson is the star of the Lions defensive line. He had 14.5 sacks last year and already has three in the first two games of this season.

DJ Wonnum is the other starting edge with second round pick Derrick Moore on the bench along with another rookie, the undrafted Eric O’Neill. Ahmed Hassanein was inactive last Thursday.

Tyler Lacy is also listed as an edge but he’s 300 pounds and also plays inside. In addition, the Lions also have former first round pick Payton Turner, but he’s on injured reserve.

The starters on the interior are Alim McNeill and Tyleik Williams. McNeill’s importance is evident by the fact that he’s easily Detroit’s highest paid defensive player.

Sixth round rookie Skyler Gill-Howard provides depth off the bench along with Levi Onwuzurike. Mekhi Wingo is also on the roster but was inactive against the Bills.

Linebackers

The linebacker unit is anchored by all-pro Jack Campbell, who had 176 tackles last season. Derrick Barnes is the other starter and he’s had an effective start to the season with 13 tackles, two pass breakups, two sacks and an interception in the first two games.

Depth comes from Trevor Nowaske, Malcolm Rodriguez and the experienced Devin White. Fourth round pick Jimmy Rolder has been inactive so far, though.

Defensive Backs

The Lions have serious issues in their secondary, which is the main reason they have given up the second highest yardage total and points total in the first two games.

Safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, each of whom were pro bowlers in 2024, began the year on the PUP list, so the Jets have known for some time Detroit would be undermanned in the secondary for this game.

However, Avonte Maddox, who was filling in, suffered a season-ending foot injury in the Bills game and, as if that wasn’t bad enough, his replacement Thomas Harper is also out of Sunday’s game due to an ankle issue.

Options that remain include ex-Jets Chuck Clark and Jalen Mills. Clark started the first two games but Mills was only just added to the practice squad a few days ago. Offseason addition Christian Izien may need to step up, while undrafted rookie Bishop Fitzgerald is also an option.

The Lions are theoretically at full strength in terms of the cornerback position but their starting trio – DJ Reed, Rock Ya-Sin and slot corner Roger McCreary all lack size which could be an issue against some of the multiple tight end looks the Jets run.

Fifth round rookie Keith Abney II, Khalil Dorsey and Ennis Rakestraw Jr. provide depth at corner.

Special Teams

Kicker Jake Bates has made all 10 of his kicks so far this season, but he missed nine in 2025. He has a big leg but was just 4-for-9 from beyond 50 last season.

Punter Jack Fox, a pro bowler in 2020 and 2024, is off to a solid start after his numbers dropped off a bit in 2025.

Longtime return specialist (and former Jet) Kalif Raymond is now with the Bears, so the Lions have Kennedy and Saylors returning kicks. Kennedy has handled punts so far, with the kickoff duties shared. Nobody has broken a long one yet this year.

Martin and Dorsey are the team’s primary punt gunners and Martin leads the team with four special teams tackles so far this season. Nowaske, Vaki and Saylors were productive in kick coverage last year.

item.title: Arch Manning family tree: How Texas QB is related to Vols legend Peyton Manning
item.description: Arch Manning and the top-ranked Longhorns will make their Rocky Top debut Saturday when they head to Knoxville to play Peyton Manning's alma mater.
item.content:encoded:
Arch Manning and the top-ranked Longhorns will make their Rocky Top debut Saturday when they head to Knoxville for a highly anticipated showdown — and one of the week's top matchups — with the No. 13 Volunteers at noon ET on Saturday, Sept. 26.

Manning's first full season as Texas' starting quarterback last season came with a ton of hype and, arguably, impossible-to-achieve expectations.

The resulting up-and-down season ended on a momentum-building note heading into 2026, as he led the Longhorns to a 7-1 record, including a bowl win, in their final eight games. He threw for over 2,000 yards and 15 touchdowns in that span.

Now, in Year 2, the Longhorn quarterback once again has high expectations surrounding his name: He is a contender not only for the Heisman Trophy, but also the top overall pick in the upcoming NFL draft. If anything, it shouldn't be anything new for the 6-4 quarterback, who has dealt with such expectations for much of his playing career — given the fact he's a member of football's most well-known families.

All in the family: Arch Manning looks for bragging rights over Peyton in Texas-Tennessee

More: Arch Manning's first game at Tennessee forced Peyton Manning to choose

"Going through those rough times, (I) learned a lot about myself. I’ve become a better man because of it and hopefully a better player," Manning said at SEC Media Days in July. "Don’t want to repeat that game."

Texas coach Steve Sarkisian called his quarterback a "very dangerous player" at SEC Media Days because of the adversity he weathered last season with the Longhorns, who just missed the postseason.

Here's what you need to know about Arch Manning's family tree as he gets ready to start his second full-season starting at Texas:

Arch Manning family tree

Who is Arch Manning's grandfather?

Arch Manning is the grandson and namesake of former Mississippi and New Orleans Saints quarterback Archie Manning .

Archie Manning was the No. 2 overall pick in the 1971 NFL Draft out of Ole Miss by the Saints, with whom he spent the first 11 years of his NFL career. He would later play for the Houston Oilers and Minnesota Vikings to finish out his 13-year NFL career.

Archie Manning, who threw for nearly 24,000 career passing yards and 125 touchdowns, has been in the news recently with his grandson.

Who is Arch Manning's dad?

Arch Manning's father is Cooper Manning, the eldest son of Archie Manning and older brother to Peyton and Eli Manning (Arch Manning's uncles).

Cooper Manning — like his father — committed to Ole Miss to play college football, albeit at wide receiver instead of quarterback. However, his career with the Rebels never took off: he was diagnosed with spinal stenosis before he arrived at Ole Miss.

REQUIRED READING: Who is the most athletic Manning? Ranking football family by speed

Who are Arch Manning's uncles?

Arch Manning is the nephew of legendary college football and NFL quarterbacks Peyton and Eli Manning.

Peyton Manning was the first to break from Manning family tradition, choosing to commit to Tennessee over Ole Miss. In his time on Rocky Top, Peyton Manning quickly became one of the all-time greatest players in Tennessee history, throwing for 11,201 passing yards and 89 touchdowns. He posted a record of 39-6 as a starter.

Eli Manning played college football at Ole Miss from 1999 to 2003, a career that saw him become one of the all-time great Rebels quarterbacks. He set the program's all-time passing records with 10,119 yards and 81 career touchdowns, marks which stood until Jaxson Dart surpassed them in 2024.

Both Peyton and Eli Manning exhausted their college eligibility before being selected No. 1 overall in the 1998 and 2004 NFL drafts, respectively.

Eli Manning spent all 16 seasons of his NFL career with the New York Giants, who traded for him on draft night in 1998 after he was selected by the San Diego Chargers. He went on to win two Super Bowls with the Giants, both of which came against New England's Tom Brady, long considered Peyton Manning's top rival and greatest contemporary in the NFL.

Peyton Manning spent his 18-year Hall of Fame career in the NFL with the Indianapolis Colts and the Denver Broncos. He won a Super Bowl title with each: in the 2006 season with the Colts and again in 2015, with the Broncos. The former Vols quarterback, who was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame as a first-ballot inductee in 2021, ranks third all-time in NFL career passing yards (71,940) and threw for 539 career touchdowns.

Who is Peyton Manning's son?

Peyton's son Marshall is a high school freshman quarterback at Baylor School (Tenn.)

Manning transferred to Baylor ahead of his eighth grade year from Denver and is serving as Baylor’s backup quarterback this season.

item.title: Outlining a plan to address the Washington Commanders’ secondary issues
item.description: Hogs Haven’s John Portis outlines how he would resolve the Commanders secondary woes for Sunday’s game vs. Seattle.
item.content:encoded:
Things have not gone according to plan for the Washington Commanders and their secondary through the first two weeks of the season. The idea of frequent and disguised pressures shouldering the bulk of the burden for the defensive backs is not sustainable if teams can slow the pressure and exploit coverage lapses, and there have been plenty to exploit. As many fans will tell you, the ship has sailed on any significant personnel additions at this point in the season, but in this article I will outline how defensive coordinator Daronte Jones could try to fix the issues in the secondary with the players he currently has on the roster.

The most difficult part of the plan is it requires the coaching staff to make personnel changes instead of dispensing platitudes and focusing on communication and leveling up. It also needs to happen quickly, before the team is 0-4 to start the season. Listening to Daronte Jones’ last press conference, I don’t know if they feel the same urgency to make the necessary changes.

Still, here is what I think Jones should do if he decides to switch things up, using Hogs Haven writer MattInBrisVegas’s wonderful Stats and Snaps series as our guide.

Bench

Mike Sainristil

After the first two games, Mike Sainristil currently has a 153.7 allowed passer rating, is ranked 94th out of 94 CBs by PFF, and is coming off a atrocious performance last week where Pro Football Reference assigned him 3.07 Y/Cov Snp.

Hogs Haven’s Mark Tyler has some interesting ideas on what to do with Mikey, but with the goal of improving the secondary immediately, I am going with the bench option. It might be wise for Jones to assign Sainristil nothing but slot reps in practice and see if he can work his way back into the lineup, but for now he needs to sit.

Out

Nick Cross

Initially, I had a different version of this plan put together, one that included Cross as a key piece of the puzzle, but with the news he was hospitalized after the Cowboys game and ruled out completely on Wednesday, I think Commanders fans should not plan on him being part of the solution for a couple of weeks.

So what’s the plan?

If we look at Matt’s tables from this week’s article, we can identify what positions Jones will need to fill this week versus Seattle after removing two starters.

Mike Sainristil played the majority of his snaps at LCB, but there are also some slot and box snaps that need to be accounted for as well. Nick Cross moved around the secondary but was the team’s primary slot defender. So we need to look at three different roles: LCB, Slot/Box, and FS.

LCB

Jones has already been trending towards the first move by giving Rasul Douglas more snaps last week. The veteran cornerback hasn’t been perfect, but PFR has him with a more palatable 97.4 allowed passer rating. Matt’s data from the Cowboys game tells us that Douglas had a bad day in coverage, allowing 5 targets and 4 receptions for 52 yds in 18 coverage snaps (2.89 Y/Cov Snp), but I would think a good chunk of the allowed yards came from this play where he read the route wrong.

While this certainly is not what you want to see, the remainder of his reps were better and Douglas would be a step up for what we have seen from Sainristil on the boundary. The thought would be to have Rasul work almost completely on the outside, as he has done for most of his career and find another option at the slot position.

Slot/Box

Last season, when corner Jeff Odukah went out with a concussion, the Vikings elevated Fabian Moreau from the practice squad to the active roster. The 32-year-old veteran did surprisingly well playing limited snaps there, posting very respectable containment numbers (0.51 Y/Cov Snap) and a 54.6 allowed passer rating on 152 coverage snaps.

Moreau was brought in as a break glass in case of emergency option as the veteran who knows Jones’ system after two seasons with the Vikings. Unfortunately, I think we have reached that point. Limiting Fabian’s snaps would be important, but the 6’0”, 204-pound Moreau could provide some solid ones as a big nickel.

Jeremy Reaves was initially one of my players to bench, as his 158.7 allowed pass rating is one of the worst in the league, but with Nick Cross sidelined, there is a void in the total snap count for the secondary. The fix is to play Reaves in the box with little to no snaps at the free safety position. Jeremy is still a very physical player and can trigger downhill in run support and the short-to-intermediate parts of the field.

I don’t love this solution, but it could work until Cross returns from injury.

Free Safety

Here is where the plan gets a little thin. The team never accounted for the free safety role in their roster planning during the offseason with Martin or Harris potentially filling the role but ultimately ended up demoting Martin, releasing Harris, and going with Jeremy Reaves in their place. With Reaves relegated to the box, the team needs to find another player at free safety.

Tyler Owens has been a career special teamer so far, but still might be the best option to replace Reaves and Cross in the deep part of the field. He has the size, speed, and athleticism, but in his one chance last season he looked lost in his assignments.

The thing to note here is that Owens played heavily up by the line of scrimmage and in the slot, instead of in a free safety role. In fact, according to Matt’s write-up for last season’s matchup versus the Chiefs he played none at the position.

In a role that keeps the play in front of him, limits his reads, and allows him to utilize his range, Owens could potentially perform significantly better.

Quan Martin hasn’t been quite as bad as Sainristil through two games, with a 118.7 allowed passer rating per Pro Football Reference. The catch is he has played about half the total number of snaps as Mikey. PFF has him ranked 83rd out of 84 safeties. He was also initially on my bench list as well but also gets a pass with Cross out as the team will likely need him here for two high safety looks, if they decide not to play Reaves there.

Coaching & Communication

The Washington Commanders decided to retain defensive backs/safeties coach Tom Donatell during the offseason while promoting William Gay from assistant coach to defensive backs/cornerbacks coach. The two decisions were surprising given the secondary’s performance last year and Donatell’s previous track record with the San Diego Chargers. Daronte Jones’ previous ties to defensive coordinator Ed Donatell may have added a layer of familiarity after LSU safeties coach Jake Olsen changed his mind about accepting an offer to join Washington’s coaching staff. Whatever the reason, the two coaches do not seem to be successful installing coverage and communication techniques and Jones will have to take valuable time away from developing his defensive game plan to correct it.

Communication issues have been a persistent problem for Washington’s secondary, especially the last few under Dan Quinn’s direction. A good portion of the Commanders’ secondary has been here for that same length of time or longer, and the idea that issues that still exist over a full slate of offseason activities, training camp, and preseason can be corrected quickly is hard to swallow. Simplifying the defense should help, but sometimes if two people can’t communicate, they need to talk to someone else. Personnel changes could also help solve some of the issues, especially if some of the secondary can’t trust one another and Cross’s injury could give them the opportunity to shake up the group.

Dan Quinn mentioned Quan Martin and Percy Butler in his Friday presser, so their plan may rely on rolling out the same old options. We will find out Sunday, but if Daronte Jones is able to get his unit to perform, things should only get better as Cross and Amos will add more talent to the group if and when they return.

A big thank you to MattInBrisVegas for agreeing to let me piggyback off his hard work. Be sure to check in with Stats and Snaps next week to see if things went according to plan.

item.title: Future Broncos: 2 Rising Prospects to Watch in Week 4 of NCAA Football Season
item.description: Another weekend, another installment of Future Broncos. In the first three weeks, we have highlighted nine prospects from entirely different position groups. item.content:encoded:
Another weekend, another installment of Future Broncos. In the first three weeks, we have highlighted nine prospects from entirely different position groups. Moving forward, there will certainly be overlap at certain positions.

In the comments section, a few people talked about more tight ends and linebackers. That’s why two rising prospects will be on the radar this week for discussion. Without further ado, here are my trio of prospects for Broncos Country to watch today in Week 4 of the college football season.

Luke Reynolds — Tight End — Virginia Tech

Oregon standout Jamari Johnson was the first tight end I mentioned as a potential first-round target for the Broncos next April. Truth be told, I wasn’t planning to do another tight end so early on in the season. However, after his dominant performance against Maryland last week and start to the ‘26 season, Virginia Tech standout Luke Reynolds is worth mentioning.

Reynolds began his collegiate career at Penn State. As a freshman in 2024, he played in sixteen games and had just nine catches for 111 yards and one touchdown. That’s not impressive production, but it’s worth nothing he was backing up future first-round pick Tyler Warren.

As a sophomore, he split time with two other players in a heavy rotation at the position. His production as a receiver went up a smidge and finished the year with 26 catches for 257 yards. He was also a key inline blocker for running backs Nicholas Singleton and Kaytron Allen to bolster Penn State’s rushing attack.

A coaching change with the Nittany Lions coupled with many of their key offensive starters going to the 2026 NFL Draft were big reasons Reynolds transferred to Virginia Tech this year. The decision looks to be wise with respect to his draft stock which is now soaring.

In three games with the Hokies thus far, he has 25 catches for 265 yards and 4 touchdowns. He is coming off a 12 catch, 107-yard, and one touchdown performance against the Terrapins. It took a few years, but everyone watching is beginning to see why he was the nation’s top potential recruit several years ago.

He may not be a top-tier athlete but is savvy finding spots against zone coverage and has the toughness to break tackles and create yards after the catch. Prospects who can move the chains, be a threat in the redzone, and propel the run game with good blocking are in high demand across the league. If Reynolds keeps this level of play up, he should easily be a Top 50 selection next Spring as an early declarant. In my opinion, he is a terrific fit for Head Coach Sean Payton’s offense. Reynolds can do it all.

You can catch the junior in action when the undefeated Hokies head on the road take on Boston College for an ACC matchup this morning.

Ben Roberts — Linebacker — Texas Tech

Last year, readers of Future Broncos were definitely high on linebacker Jacob Rodriguez. Watching him, you would have undoubtedly seen his teammate Ben Roberts making his fair share of plays too. One of the best off-ball linebacker prospects in the nation, Roberts is hoping to build upon a junior season where he posted 90 tackles and 4 interceptions.

Entering his fourth year as a starter for the Red Raiders, Roberts is an imposing prospect at 6’3” and 245 pounds. That’s NFL ready size. If prospects who force turnovers are high on your list, the fifth-year senior is one of the best prospects this cycle. Over his collegiate career, he has half a dozen interceptions to his name and nearly an identical number of forced fumbles. Quite simply, #13 is a turnover magnet.

For those wanting to see better coverage chops from Denver’s linebacking corps, Roberts really stands out. He was a multi-star athlete in high school and played defensive back. With his safety background, it shouldn’t be a s surprise he touts top-notch coverage skills as a linebacker. That being said, no prospect is perfect and there are a few things he needs to work on.

This season, I’m hoping to see some improvement and consistency in the run game. He added weight and strength this offseason to do better at shedding blocks. He has over 300 career tackles, but very few of those have been behind the line of scrimmage. I believe he can do a much better job with diagnosis and his pursuit angles. In 2025, he had nine missed tackles—but his sub-8-percent missed tackle rate is slightly better than average for the position.

For whatever reason, I’ve seen Roberts ranked as a Day 3 prospect on a lot of consensus boards. That seems pretty wild. I’d wager a four-year starter that has played at an incredibly high level with his traits and production will be a Top 64 selection in the ‘27 NFL Draft—even with the rough edges and flaws that need rounding out.

If you’re still banging the “Broncos need to draft an inside linebacker!” drum, you can catch Roberts in action when the eleventh ranked Red Raiders host Sam Houston this morning. It’ll be a cakewalk game for them, and I expect Roberts to put on a dominant performance.

item.title: Chicago Bears Week 3 Flashbacks: Minnesota Miracle, Windy City Flyer, and More
item.description: Hope aboard the Gridiron Time Machine with @iamcogs and take a trip down down Bears memory lane!
item.content:encoded:
It’s week 3, and as always, we have some hallmark games from the past to uncover!

1.) 1985, Bears @ Vikings: McMahon’s Miracle in Minny

The 1985 Bears season is filled with memorable moments, but one of the first came on a Thursday night in Minnesota.

Jim McMahon was dealing with back spasms and an infection in his right leg, leaving Steve Fuller to start with Chicago looking to improve to 3-0. The offense struggled without McMahon, and midway through the third quarter the Bears found themselves trailing 17-9.

Mike Ditka finally turned to his injured quarterback.

McMahon’s first pass went 70 yards for a touchdown to Willie Gault. His second went 25 yards to Dennis McKinnon for another score.

Seven pass attempts into his night, McMahon connected with McKinnon again for a 43-yard touchdown.

Just like that, a 17-9 deficit had become a 30-17 Bears lead.

McMahon finished 8-of-15 for 236 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions, while Gault recorded 146 receiving yards and McKinnon added 133 yards and two scores. Chicago held on for a 33-24 win.

The victory moved the Bears to 3-0 on their way to a 15-1 season and, eventually, a dominant run through the playoffs and a Super Bowl XX championship.

Before all of that, though, an injured Jim McMahon came off the bench and completely flipped a game in a matter of minutes.

2.) 2010, Bears vs. Packers: Devin Hester is still ridiculous

By 2010, the NFL had learned a pretty simple lesson when it came to Devin Hester.

Don’t kick him the football.

Hester entered Chicago’s Monday Night Football matchup with Green Bay without a return touchdown in nearly three years. With both teams sitting at 2-0, the Packers built a 10-0 lead before Jay Cutler found Greg Olsen late in the first half to get Chicago back into the game.

The Bears still trailed 10-7 entering the fourth quarter.

Then Hester finally broke through.

He fielded a punt and raced 62 yards for a touchdown, giving Chicago its first lead of the night and recording his first return score since 2007.

Green Bay answered and retook the lead, but Robbie Gould tied the game at 17 before the Bears defense came up with one more opportunity. Brian Urlacher stripped James Jones late in the fourth quarter, with Tim Jennings recovering the fumble in Green Bay territory.

Gould eventually drilled a 19-yard field goal with four seconds remaining to give Chicago a 20-17 victory.

The Packers did plenty to hurt themselves, committing a franchise-record 18 penalties for 152 yards, but the lasting image from the night was Hester looking like the most dangerous return man in football once again.

Chicago improved to 3-0 and eventually finished the season 11-5, winning the NFC North and reaching the NFC Championship Game.

For one night at Soldier Field, the formula was pretty simple.

Give Devin Hester the football and see what happens.

3.) 2013, Bears @ Steelers: The defense takes over

For years, Chicago’s defense had built its identity around one thing.

Taking the football away.

That trend continued into Marc Trestman’s first season as head coach, and Week 3 against the Steelers was one of the best examples.

The Bears jumped out to a 17-0 lead, helped by a D.J. Williams strip-sack that set up an early touchdown. Then the defense started scoring points of its own.

Major Wright intercepted Ben Roethlisberger and returned it 38 yards for a touchdown, giving Chicago a 24-3 advantage.

Pittsburgh battled all the way back, eventually cutting the lead to 27-23 in the fourth quarter behind 406 passing yards from Roethlisberger and 196 receiving yards from Antonio Brown.

Chicago finally answered with a Jay Cutler touchdown pass to Earl Bennett.

Then the defense put the game away.

Lance Briggs knocked the ball free while sacking Roethlisberger, and Julius Peppers picked it up and rumbled 42 yards for another Bears defensive touchdown.

Chicago left Pittsburgh with a 40-23 victory and a 3-0 record.

The final numbers tell the story. Pittsburgh outgained the Bears 459-258, but Chicago forced five turnovers, committed none and scored 23 points off Pittsburgh giveaways.

It may not have been the cleanest win, but it was a familiar formula for Bears fans.

Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs.

Last week, Sportico published its ranking of highest-paid NFL coaches. The list included both Harbaughs: brothers Jim and John. There were also two Kevins: O’Connell and Stefanski. But the name repetition on NFL sidelines doesn’t stop there.

Last Sunday’s game between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the Cleveland Browns was the first game in NFL history with two head coaches named Todd. Incredibly, the Bucs’ Todd Bowles and the Browns’ Todd Monken also share the middle name Robert. It was the Todd Robert Bowl.

The web of shared names among NFL head coaches turns out to be far more complex than anyone could have imagined.

You can read the full essay at Club Sportico. Here’s an excerpt ✍️:

A whopping 25 NFL head coaches share a name—first, middle, or last—with another head coach. There are six Mikes, four Roberts, four Patricks, three Williams, three Johns, etc. And some share multiple names. Below are all the connections mapped out:

Because of this web, NFL head coach name “bowl” games are much more common than you’d think. For example, this season’s kickoff game was a rematch of Super Bowl XL, and also a Mike Bowl, between the Seattle Seahawks’ Mike Macdonald and the New England Patriots’ Mike Vrabel.

In Week 2, each of those Mikes participated in another Mike Bowl when Vrabel coached against the Pittsburgh Steelers’ Mike McCarthy, while Macdonald coached against the Arizona Cardinals’ Mike LaFleur. At the same time, there was a third Mike Bowl in San Francisco between the 49ers and Dolphins—Kyle Shanahan and Jeff Hafley each have the middle name Michael!

For this week’s Sunday Night Football, we have probably the most exciting bowl game of the season, as the Los Angeles Rams, led by Sean Patrick McVay, take on the Denver Broncos, led by Patrick Sean Payton, in the Sean Patrick Bowl. Two Super Bowl-winning coaches. Two of the five highest-paid coaches. And the most unlikely from a name perspective.

How unlikely? As the data guy, I had to dig deeper.

Middle names are not tracked by the Social Security Administration. According to a YouGov poll, though, middle names are given after relatives far more frequently than first names, so I think we can safely assume that common first names are at least equally common as middle names.

In 1975, the average of McVay’s and Payton’s birth years, 0.5% of male babies were named Patrick and 1.2% were named some variant of Sean. Multiplying those together, and then multiplying by two, we get that about 1 in every 8,333 babies were named Sean Patrick or Patrick Sean. Using that estimate, in a randomly selected group of 32 males from that generation, there’s about a 1 in 140,000 chance that at least two would be named Sean Patrick. For comparison, the Todd Robert Bowl was only 1 in ~29,000.

All in all, there are 12 matchups this year that I’d consider “true bowl games,” where the two head coaches have either the same first name, the same middle name, or the same last name (I’m counting the Sean Patrick Bowl, because Payton is generally referred to as Sean Payton, even though Sean is actually his middle name).

Gven current trends in baby naming, it’s only downhill from here.

Sadly, these names are rapidly becoming less popular. Michael, for instance, which peaked at 4.7% of all baby boys in 1969, is down to just 0.4%. John has undergone a similar trajectory, once accounting for more than 4% of all newly born males, but now just 0.4%. Seans (and Shawns) and Patricks have dipped even further to 0.08% and 0.03% last year, respectively. New Todds are essentially extinct, having dropped outside the top 1,000 names back in 2014.

But it’s not just these particular names that are in decline—it’s all “common” names. Fifty years ago, 41.1% of all baby boys were given a name in the top 25 most popular names. Last year, that was only 14.4%—an astonishing drop. So 2026 is likely the peak of NFL head coach name bowl games.

item.title: Big Blue View mailbag: It’s all quarterback all the time
item.description: The mail’s here! Questions, answers about the Giants.
item.content:encoded:
Ed Helinski asks: What’s the Giants Plan C if Jameis Winston isn’t the answer for whatever reason?

Ed says: Ed, how many times actually have a realistic Plan C at quarterback? The reality is that if you are down to your third quarterback, things are not going to go well.

There are 32 NFL teams. Even if every quarterback is healthy, there aren’t 32 good starting quarterbacks in the league. By extension, there aren’t 32 good backup quarterbacks. The truth is nobody ever wants to see their third quarterback play — that guy is a baseball cap-wearing third quarterback or practice squad guy for a reason.

That said, I’m sure the Giants will look around at practice squads, a street free agent like Jimmy Garoppolo, and trade options.

Considering how many quarterbacks have gotten hurt in the first two weeks of the season, though, how many teams are going to be willing to trade away someone they consider to be a capable backup? At this point, that’s GM malpractice.

The Giants just gave Jameis Winston a two-year, $13 milliion extension. They didn’t do that to replace him as soon as they need a backup quarterback.

Todd Graf asks: Do the OC and DC come down to the locker room at halftime or do they work the 2nd half game plan from the booth? Thought about this with Jameis taking over for Jaxson and his 1st half struggles…. And also because there isn’t much time at halftime.

Ed says: Todd, let me clarify that to my knowledge defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson works from the sideline.

To answer your question, all of the coaches who work from upstairs make a beeline for the locker room at halftime. At MetLife Stadium, that means taking the elevator from the sixth floor down to the ground floor and then hustling down the tunnel to the room for a brief interaction with John Harbaugh, players, and other coaches, then back upstairs before the second half starts.

Ted Schwartz asks: All of the cards appeared to be aligning for what would be an exciting season where I finally could watch all of the games while being surrounded by fellow fans! Alas, the football gods have struck down that excitement.

Watching the devastating injury to Dart and the massive blow it struck to this team for the season, leaves me wondering about accountability within the team. I know football is a dangerous sport and any player can get injured through no fault of their own or their teammates. But this injury appears to me to be squarely on the shoulders of the Left and Right tackle who both got beat badly on the same play and left their quarterback exposed to the vicious punishment his body received. 

Does this affect the team chemistry with some players feeling if even one of them did their job properly their quarterback would not be injured and the team would not be in this position. Dart stayed in the pocket, did not put himself unnecessarily in harms way and trusted and relied on his teammates, who failed him. Does the team discuss this as a whole, are the players spoken to individually, is there any penalty for them within the team environment or is it just chalked up as an unfortunate football injury. 

Have either of them spoken out about their role in this injury? Of course they didn’t mean for it to happen and Im sure they were trying their hardest not to let it happen. But they let their quarterback down, let their team down, and let their fans down.

Ed says: Ted, trying to assign blame to other players for a guy getting injured is not constructive, and not something teams or players do. I did not get an opportunity to speak to Andrew Thomas or Jermaine Eluemunor when I was there on Wednesday. Both guys are among the best in the league at their jobs, and are highly-respected inside that locker room. Players get beat sometimes. The guys on the other side are also professionals. It happens. This “they let their quarterback down” stuff is way over the top.

Spoken to individually? Penalty within the team? I am sure the team has looked at the film and understands why the play happened, but these guys aren’t children.

I think you are looking for some type of team divide or finger-pointing that simply doesn’t exist.

I think the video below from Chris Simms is instructive. I agree with him that this play was in “disarray” before the ball was snapped. That doesn’t mean I am blaming Dart, either. Dart’s not the first quarterback to get sandwiched by multiple defenders, and he won’t be the last.

Bob Donnelly asks: How does the loss of Jaxson Dart impact your projection for Giant’s 2026 win/loss record?

Ed says: Bob, as Big Blue View readers probably (should?) know I predicted 9-8, calling that the “most optimistic” prediction I could make for 2026.

I would think 9-8 without Dart would be a fantastic season. I think right now it would be hard to complain about seven wins.

The next three weeks — winnable games against the Titans, Cardinals, Commanders — will tell us more about what to expect.

Patrick Morris asks: The injury to Jaxson Dart is awful. His play when he has been available has been inspiring. But, the season without him is not as hopeful, and the odds of the Giants having a high draft pick have gone up. 

If the Giants end the season with a poor record, but an opportunity to draft one of the top 3 QBs in the upcoming draft class…do they take it?

Ed says: I don’t know what they would do. But, I think the answer would be no. My answer would definitely be no.

John Urbielewicz asks: The inside linebacker play against the Rams was horrible. One could make an argument that Micah McFadden is our best inside linebacker at this time. I think Arvell Reese is going to be a great player in this league, but right now with Brian Burns missing time, I would move Arvell to the end rusher and play McFadden.

Your thoughts?

Ed says: John, no. Arvell Reese is an inside linebacker. That is what the Giants drafted him to be. That is where he has practiced since the spring. That is where he is best.

The Giants align him outside occasionally to change the look of the defense and try to create desirable matchups. Maybe that happens a little more frequently with Burns out, but moving Reese to the edge and starting McFadden is an overreation.

Chris Chianese asks: Ed, in your “Ride with Winston” article it left me thinking … finally there is someone showing some common sense and reality with the Dart injury and where we are with the QB for the Gs this season. First and foremost, Harbaugh and Schoen didn’t sign Winston to an extension to move on from him if Dart got injured. I suppose a person could take issue with Winston being the backup considering he is such a different QB than Dart. So, in other words, the Gs offense will need to be revamped to accommodate Winston’s abilities. So my question is, which QBs out there that are free agents or on a practice squad, most emulate what Dart’s abilities to sign as a backup to Winston? Milton? Hooker?Or, for continuity in the 2026 season, does signing Jimmy Garoppolo make more sense as a backup to Winston since Jimmy G is more like Winston?

Ed says: Chris, I honestly don’t think emulating Dart has anything to do with it. I think the point is to find the player the Giants believe can do the best job helping them win games if he has to play. If that is a quarterback who offers the chance to use the quarterback run game, fine. If it is more of a pocket passer, fine.

John Harbaugh has succeeded with Joe Flacco, a pocket passer, at quarterback. He also succeeded with a running quarterback — Lamar Jackson.

Matt Nagy, Greg Roman, Brian Callahan have worked with both types.

Submit a question

Have a Giants-related question? E-mail it to bigblueview@gmail.com and it might be featured in our weekly mailbag.

item.title: Bills vs. Chargers predictions: Buffalo’s offense may dominate in Week 3
item.description: Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills’ well-positioned to dismantle the struggling Los Angeles Chargers in Week 3
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills are on a heater right now, with quarterback Josh Allen playing incredible football at a clip that has him as the current odds-on favorite to win NFL MVP honors for the 2026 NFL season. Now 2-0 and with impressive offensive showings against both the Houston Texans and Detroit Lions, the Bills are set to welcome the woebegone Los Angeles Chargers to cozy Highmark Stadium.

Things could get out of hand quickly if recent game history is an indication. Will Buffalo’s offense continue its dominant ways in Week 3? It’s trending that way, especially if Allen, running back James Cook III, and tight end Dalton Kincaid continue playing elite football.

Many consider this a trap game for the Bills given the situation. However, Buffalo is a much better team than either the Arizona Cardinals or Las Vegas Raiders, which both defeated the Chargers by identical 26-14 scores. That said, Buffalo has its own less-than-ideal identical pair from its first two wins: the defense gave up 31 points in each matchup.

Will current trends prevail or is Buffalo headed for a trap? Below, we dive into a few bold predictions for Bills vs. Chargers in Week 3 using data and odds courtesy of FanDuel Sportsbook.

Josh Allen features early and often Week 3

Through two games, Josh Allen has nine total touchdowns, which includes five passing scores. He’s off to a land-speed-record pace this season, but is it sustainable? It should be at least through Week 3 thanks to a reeling Chargers team.

Los Angeles has given up a combined 46-of-66 for 530 yards with four touchdowns and one interception to quarterbacks Jacoby Brissett and Kurt Cousins. I like Allen to surpass that two-game average of 265 yards and two passing touchdowns, perhaps even besting the 23-of-33 pass/attempts average.

As of publishing, FanDuel Sportsbook lists Allen’s passing yards total at over 238.5 (-115)/under 238.5 (-115). That over feels like a given this week.

Yes, simply picking Allen to surpass what are essentially two-game average marks against LAC isn’t a bold prediction. Instead, I like the odds of Allen throwing for north of 300 yards (+350 at FanDuel), with at least three passing touchdowns (+250 at FanDuel) and at no less than one rushing score (anytime -140 | +450 to score 2+ at FanDuel). I also think Allen will again claim the game’s first score (not a passing TD) as a rusher with a tone-setting touchdown (+550 at FanDuel).

Despite the potential for wide receivers DJ Moore and Keon Coleman to both sit out Week 3, there will be plenty of touchdown options, all of whom Allen is well-versed with at wide receiver, tight end, and running back. that includes the expected return of dynamic dual-threat running back Ty Johnson, who’s proven to be a third-down specialist as a receiver.

If Buffalo wins the coin toss, look for them to take the ball on offense again — perhaps a nod to the ‘90s Super Bowl Bills teams that sought to bury opponents with an early lead. Head coach Joe Brady has decided to let Josh cook early this season, and it’s worked with aplomb. Expect to see Allen featured early and often in Week 3.

Dalton Kincaid dominates in Week 3

You might not see this as a bold prediction, especially if Moore and Coleman are sidelined, however Buffalo does have numerous, sometimes overlooked, options to play a featured role as receiver. Week 1, Dalton Kincaid was second on the team in targets (6), co-led the team in catches (5), and led all pass catchers in yards with 130 through the air. Kincaid followed that up with a Week 2 performance featuring seven catches on eight targets for 95 yards — all three serving as team leads — plus his first touchdown of the 2026 season.

In Week 3, Kincaid should feast again as a receiver. Kincaid has the fifth-best odds as a touchdown scorer (non-passing), with anytime odds of +185 at FanDuel. Concerning receiving yards, Kincaid’s O/U with FanDuel sits at O 56.6 (-114)/U 56.5 (-114). It would be far more shocking to seem him flirt with that under. I’d roll with the odds that Kincaid surpasses 100 yards in Week 3 (+470 at FanDuel) and 7+ receptions (+400 at FanDuel).

As a deep threat, Kincaid has been a serious problem for defenses of late. In fact, as of publishing, Kincaid has the best odds through FanDuel of hauling in a 15+ yard reception (-550), a 20+ yard reception (-210), and a 30+ yard reception (+190). So far this season, when you think of Kincaid, you envision long receptions downfield no matter who’s covering him.

James Cook 1st RB to humble LAC in 2026

There’s been a lot of forgettable football out of the Chargers through two losses, but their rushing defense has been fairly stout. Games against the Raiders’ Ashton Jeanty (21 carries, 48 yards; 4 catches, 15 yards) and Cardinals RB1A Tyler Allgeier (17 carries, 61 yards; 2 catches, 9 yards) and rookie RB1B Jeremiyah Love (11 carries, 41 yards, 1 TD; 2 catches 9 yards) prove that Los Angeles’ front seven is serious about stopping the run.

That’s good defense against very capable backs, however, James Cook is on a different level as the reigning NFL rushing champ. Still a somewhat overlooked player in the league, Cook has had a decent start to his 2026 season. I expect him to get plenty of touches in Week 3, which should lead to a bunch of yards and a score or two as one of the most dynamic dual-threats in today’s game.

Cook is a featured back, but someone who has seen his workload reduced simply due to the team’s third-down preference to roll with Ty Johnson. As mentioned earlier, Johnson should be back this weekend. Will that eat into Cook’s snap count and, ultimately, his touches? I see a lot of that depending on how diverse a game plan the offense deploys for Cook against LA.

Cook seems primed for an explosion of offense on Sunday, perhaps totaling a new season high in carries. Interestingly, Cook has the current best odds with FanDuel of scoring 2+ touchdowns (+310), which sounds like others also believe he’s going to be a big part of Sunday’s game. To that end, Cook also has the most favorable odds of scoring a touchdown at any point in the first half (+135 at FanDuel) and also the second half (+160 at FanDuel).

Like many of his teammates, it’s true that Cook could head to the sideline early if Buffalo builds a huge lead in the second half. I’m still willing to bet that he gets a lot of run on Sunday, in an effort to really test how good the Chargers are at stopping the ground game.

Remember, Cook is always one cut away from a house call, which means he gets top billing as the favorite to finish with the most rushing yards (-185 at FanDuel). Is it too bold to say that Cook should flirt with 90+ rushing yards (+132 at FanDuel) against the Chargers? Again, one carry always has the potential to get Cook better than halfway there.

Fair warning: As of publishing, Cook sits at O/U 79.4 total rushing yards (-114). Los Angeles’ run defense is not to be so easily dismissed. Pointing back to the RB receiving stats above, the Chargers are also equally adept at keeping backs in check as a pass-catching threat. Currently through FanDuel, as a receiver Cook is O 1.5 (-154)/U 1.5 (+116) for receptions and O/U 10.5 (-114) for receiving yards. Do you like the odds that one screen pass goes the distance? Maybe you also like the odds that Cook accumulates 50+ receiving yards (+1280 at FanDuel).

The trick on Sunday comes if Brady and Allen find a better path toward utilizing Cook as a receiver. All told, I say Cook bests FanDuel’s current projection for his combined rushing and receiving yards at O/U 94.5 (-114).

item.title: Dexter Lawrence is adding, among many things, personality to the Bengals defense
item.description: This Bengals’ defensive line is having fun feasting and trash talking.
item.content:encoded:
Zac Taylor is in a unique position. He’s the head coach of the Bengals and their offensive play-caller.

In his position, Taylor, like a CEO, is also in charge of managing this team’s personalities. Most of those personalities have been on offense in Taylor’s tenure.

Now, the defense has some. Not only is the Bengals’ defense revived. It has personality, especially up front and with Dexter Lawrence.

Lawrence is the tone-setter of the Bengals’ defense. That comes in the form of on-field production, but it also comes with having a little fun on the field trash-talking.

“He just loves it. I think he’s contributed to the personality of our defense,” Taylor said after Friday’s practice. “Not only are they talented and confident, and playing with this really good chemistry, but they’ve got a really big personality as a whole, and he’s obviously a big part of this, and that’s what’s fun.”

Lawrence was mic’d up during the Bengals’ 20-6 win over the Houston Texans in Week 2. It was incredible to listen to, with Lawrence demonstrating elite trash-talking abilities.

It’s something we haven’t really seen from a Bengals’ defense in quite some time. The S.W.A.T. Team had personality back in the 80s, but Bengals’ defenses since really haven’t it… until now.

“With the mic’d up stuff, everybody gets to see kind of what we see from him, (defensive tackle) Jonathan Allen, and everybody kind of combining together,” Taylor said. “And it probably gets a couple of the other guys out of their shell a little bit.”

Don’t be surprised if you see other mic’d-up segments and soundbites from the Bengals or NFL Films showcasing Lawrence and the Bengals’ defensive line trash-talking their opponents. The Bengals’ defensive line is getting a lot of attention. They have talented players, but they also have players with personalities.

item.title: Brian Daboll downplays revenge as motivation for Titans-Giants game
item.description: Titans offensive coordinator Brian Daboll will be coaching against the team that fired him when he faces the Giants on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
Titans offensive coordinator Brian Daboll will be coaching against the team that fired him when he faces the Giants on Sunday. He says that's not particularly important.

Daboll, who was hired as Giants head coach in 2022 and fired last year, said he can set aside any emotions associated with facing his former team and just focus on doing his job.

"I've faced a lot of former teams before," Daboll said. "It's a one-week season every week, so you've got to put everything you got into it. You've got to get ready for scheme, new coordinators on their end, different players. As simple as it sounds, that's what it is every week in the National Football League. I have a ton of respect for the people in that organization. Very grateful for the opportunity the Mara family and Tisch family gave me. From top down to the bottom, really good people in that building. But it's about getting the players ready for a game. I've been on a number of teams that played my former teams before. But the focus is on our players."

Daboll also downplayed any idea that he has an advantage because he knows the players on the Giants, noting that they're a different team this year than they were last year. Daboll is treating Sunday like he'd treat any other game.

The undefeated Buffalo Bills are preparing for their second game at their just-opened Highmark Stadium.

The winless Chargers, meanwhile, are hoping they have discovered their low mark.

They are 0-2 for the first time in the head coaching career of Jim Harbaugh, including both his college and pro jobs. What’s more, they’re at risk of dropping to 0-3 for the first time since 2017, their first season after relocating to Los Angeles.

That was the sixth 0-3 start in the history of the Chargers franchise, and the previous two times — 2000 and 2003 — the club wound up with the No. 1 overall pick.

Read more:NFL Week 3 picks: Ravens defeat Cowboys; Rams beat Broncos

“There’s no time for us to be patient with the way we’re playing,” Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert told reporters this week.

After losing consecutive games to the Arizona Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders by identical scores of 26-14, the Chargers face a team that scored a combined 77 points in its first two games. The Bills beat the Houston Texans 36-31, then the Detroit Lions 41-31. They are favored by seven over the Chargers.

Worth noting, of course, is the Bills have surrendered 31 points in both of their games, tying them with Carolina for the second-most points allowed through the first two games.

Among the players who won’t be on the field for the Chargers on Sunday will be tight ends David Njoku and Charlie Kolar, both significant offseason acquisitions.

Njoku (fibula) is on injured reserve, which means he will miss at least four games, and Kolar (forearm) has been ruled out for the Buffalo game.

Maybe the Chargers wake up and come to life. Stranger turnarounds have happened. It’s a tall order for a group that looked hopelessly disjointed in the first two weeks to travel across the country and humble one of the hottest teams in the league.

This is a business trip,” head coach Brian Schottenheimer said Thursday. “The meetings and the walkthroughs and the practice that we’ll have [Friday], the trip to the stadium on Saturday, those are all critical parts to what we’re doing so we go into the game feeling prepared. I feel really good about the plan right now. It’s keeping these guys focused on the things that went in earlier in the week.”

Cowboys address concerns regarding playing field in Brazil – Patrik Walker, DallasCowboys.com

Reports have come out that the field Maracana Stadium might not be up to par for Sunday’s game. The Cowboys don’t seem concerned in the slightest.

CeeDee Lamb, fresh off of a huge game against those very same Commanders, racking up 153 yards and two touchdowns, including the record-setting catch from Prescott, has a much simpler view of it all.

The three-time All-Pro and five-time Pro Bowler is worrying only about what he can control.

“Let’s play,” he said when asked about the playing surface concerns. “ I don’t have questions. I’m gonna be out there, so it is what it is.”

item.title: If the Bills want to explore a Marvin Harrison Jr. trade, they should have the inside scoop on him
item.description: The Bills should have some of the most important info on Marvin Harrison Jr.
item.content:encoded:
Are the Buffalo Bills going to trade for Marvin Harrison Jr.? Heck, none of us know if the Cardinals are even going to be willing to trade him, and at this juncture, we certainly have been given no indication by the Bills — or any NFL insiders — that a trade is being explored.

Speaking of exploring, if you’re even mildly intrigued by this idea — or totally despise the thought of it — I highly encourage you to read Matt Byham’s thorough breakdown of the pros and cons of it all.

As Harrison Jr. trade speculation percolates, and it feels like it will, as any of it pertains to the Bills, it’ll be critical to remember the Bills should already have plenty of intel this young wideout.

Why?

Buffalo’s new receivers coach, Drew Terrell, was the pass game coordinator and receivers coach in Arizona the past three seasons, two of which of course correspond with the beginning of Harrison Jr.‘s NFL career with the Cardinals.

A former receiver himself, who’s only 35 years old, Terrell started in the NFL in 2018 with the Panthers as a quality control coach and spent 2020-2022 with the Commanders as an assistant receivers coach and the regular wide receiver coach in the 2021 and 2022 campaigns.

Of course, Harrison Jr. hasn’t appeared on special teams, but the Bills’ special teams coach Jeff Rodgers was in Arizona from 2019-2025 coaching special teams and with the title of assistant head coach, so he’d clearly know Harrison Jr. reasonably well too.

And we have no idea what Terrell and Rodgers think of Harrison Jr., but their close knowledge of the young wideout may either be what spurs the Bills into action on the trade front or provides the inside info to the front office that keeps the Bills away.
