item.title: 3-Point Stance: How Drake Maye can bounce back from his rough start
item.description: New England’s quarterback must rediscover what made him an MVP candidate last year.
item.content:encoded:
Two games into the 2026 season, Drake Maye has not looked like himself.

So far, the New England Patriots quarterback has thrown four interceptions to just one touchdown. Maye committed three of those turnovers in the fourth quarter alone against the Seattle Seahawks, effectively losing New England the season opener.

While the 2025 MVP runner-up’s third season hasn’t been catastrophic by any means and doesn’t warrant long-term concern, he consistently appears to be flustered in the pocket and not confident in what he’s seeing past his offensive line.

And considering the Patriots soon match up against the Jacksonville Jaguars, Buffalo Bills and the Chicago Bears before star wide receiver A.J. Brown can return, timely adjustments need to be made.

Although we can’t know exactly how Maye is processing the field, we have the resources to make estimates about why the signal-caller has struggled and how he can respond.

Embracing the short game

It’s important to note that NFL defenses are always adjusting. Therefore, Maye will have to adapt while also reestablishing the traits that made him an MVP candidate just one season ago.

Across the Patriots’ first two contests, the Seahawks and Pittsburgh Steelers defenses lined up with two-high safeties just over 50% of the time when facing Maye. Oftentimes, their play designs call for split-safety coverage, with their defense playing in cover two, four, or the dreaded cover six.

Progressing past the chains by taking the routine underneath plays forces those safeties to eventually adapt and play closer to the line of scrimmage. Excelling in the short passing game involves remaining “disciplined,” a word offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels used last week to describe how New England can adjust to how opposing teams will approach defending Maye.

The 24-year-old was efficient in that approach against Seattle, leading the reigning Super Bowl champions 7-0 at halftime, until he “lost patience.”

McDaniels added that there’s a “fine line” between taking care of the ball and taking what the defense allows while staying aggressive and making downfield plays. He called that attribute one of Maye’s greatest.

Reestablishing his poise in the pocket

Maye’s presence in the pocket is an area where the third-year quarterback has struggled to start the season, lacking the poise and composure that allowed him to methodically maneuver around pressure and throw with strong velocity and accuracy while staying in the pocket.

Yet this season, Maye often bails from the pocket when he doesn’t need to. He appears to be playing too quickly, second-guessing himself and making abrupt decisions, potentially indicating that opposing defenses are speeding him up mentally as he diagnoses what’s happening in front of him.

Pro Football Focus assigned Maye a 26.8 passing grade under pressure. A potential reason why he looks stiff in the pocket may be an effort to prevent fumbles, which he struggled with in the 2025 postseason, losing possession four times.

Still, as McDaniels alluded to, there’s a middle ground.

Recapturing those attributes begins with Maye playing more decisively without letting defenses accelerate his mental processing. That means operating the short passing game quickly and with confidence in his decision-making.

“Being decisive and believing in what you see,” head coach Mike Vrabel said on Wednesday about his quarterback. “Again, what we ask all our players to do is prepare to try to play fast and aggressively and make great decisions. 

“Ultimately, it’s [Maye’s] responsibility to distribute the football as quickly and decisively as possible in the places that it’s supposed to go, continuing not to force things and try to just create a next play on every single play.”

Preventing the underthrows

If defenses are disrupting Maye’s timing, it could also be contributing to his uncharacteristic underthrows. Operating in the pocket while questioning decisions in the moment can alter his throwing mechanics and timing, causing passes to fall short.

Two of Maye’s takeaways resulted from passes coming up short, with the final one against the Seahawks being an ill-advised decision to force a pass rather than settle for a tying field-goal attempt.

That trend could make Sunday’s matchup especially challenging as Jacksonville’s defense excels at producing turnovers. Last season, the Jaguars ranked No. 2 in the NFL with 22 total interceptions, which was just one takeaway shy of the Bears in first. Throughout their two games thus far, they already have two.

Until Maye makes the necessary adjustment, the Patriots could be playing from behind on Sunday.

“One of the best things about getting new chances every week is having to let the other ones go,” Maye said on Wednesday. “That’s one of the best things about this sport and playing this position. You have to let plays go, and you want to be attacking the next play, learning from the ones in the past and getting after the next one.

“So, I definitely think [it’s] hard to play this position when you’re thinking about a lot of different things. It’s going to be natural to think about motions, fronts, defenses, what our guys are doing, route concepts and what they’re doing versus the play we have [set] up. So, just thinking and trying to be instinctive. That’s one of the best things I learned in college is to be instinctive and try to play as fast as you can back there.”

item.title: Who will be the Detroit Lions’ MVP vs. the Jets?
item.description: Predicting who the Detroit Lions’ MVP will be against the New York Jets in Week 3.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions will be the first to tell you that good, fundamentally sound football requires the effort and skill of 11 players working in harmony. That was painfully obvious last Thursday night, when just about every play had one or two players not doing their assignment, and it made the entire team look disjointed against the Bills.

Obviously, in order to turn things around this week against the New York Jets, the Lions need to get everyone on the same page. But even if they do, it will still require heroic efforts from individuals to move Detroit to 2-1 through three weeks.

So today’s Question of the Day is:

Who will be the Lions’ MVP against the Jets?

My answer: I think this could be a big Sam LaPorta game.

This week Scottie Montgomery basically said that teams were surprisingly not double-teaming Amon-Ra St. Brown, and they were totally fine just feeding the All-Pro receiver until someone tried to stop them.

“When Saint continues to play at the level that he plays at, we will start to see something that we haven’t seen quite as much this year—maybe because of the training camp that Jameson (Williams) had—we haven’t seen as much double (teams) on Saint, which is allowing him to get some one-on-one situations,” Montgomery said.

But what he said next is where I’m going with this. Montgomery knows Jets coach Aaron Glenn knows how St. Brown can take over a game, and he’s betting he won’t let him.

“I know that that’s the last thing that he wants to see, Saint running around,” Montgomery said.

Whether the Jets will be able to contain St. Brown is a matter of opinion, but I do believe that will be their focus this week—especially considering how leaky the Jets’ middle of the defense is.

Now, that may open up opportunities for Williams deep this week, but personally, I think LaPorta will benefit most. If the Jets’ best linebackers and safeties are providing bracket coverage for St. Brown, that should leave LaPorta to operate over the rest of the field.

On top of that, I still believe LaPorta’s impact in the run game is underappreciated. The offensive line may need some extra help with a pretty strong Jets offensive line, and LaPorta could be the key to help Jahmyr Gibbs break a big run or two that could shift the game.

item.description: Here's everything you need to know about the Rams' Week 3 matchup against the Denver Broncos, including start time, TV channel and betting odds.
item.content:encoded:
It was a redemptive moment for Terrance Ferguson.

In Monday’s victory over the New York Giants, the Rams’ second-year tight end dropped passes on consecutive plays in the third quarter. But on the next drive, quarterback Matthew Stafford targeted Ferguson again — and then finished the drive with a five-yard touchdown pass to Ferguson for the final points of a 28-6 victory.

“My biggest thing is you have to make the most of your opportunities,” Ferguson said. “So when you drop the ball, you’re kind of pissed off. And when they come back to you, it just means a lot for my confidence.”

Read more:NFL Week 3 picks: Ravens defeat Cowboys; Rams beat Broncos

Ferguson caught a career-best six passes for 54 yards against the Giants. The 2025 second-round draft pick figures to have a significant role again on Sunday night when the Rams play the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High stadium.

Coach Sean McVay complimented Ferguson for responding positively after his miscues. Stafford said all players must learn to move on from their mistakes.

“I’m not going to hit everybody in stride all the time too — I’m going to miss some,” Stafford said. “We’re programmed to move on to the next one and believe in each other and trust each other and trust your fundamentals. That’s all [Ferguson] did on the touchdown catch and the other great plays he had too.

“He’s a bright spot for our team. He’s a young player that’s still coming into his own.”

Last season as a rookie, Ferguson was hindered early in the schedule because of a hamstring injury suffered during training camp. But he emerged as a productive target, catching 17 passes for 285 yards and four touchdowns as part of a tight end group that included veterans Tyler Higbee, Colby Parkinson and Davis Allen.

On Sept. 10, in the Rams’ season-opening defeat by the San Francisco 49ers, Ferguson was targeted only once. Against the Giants, he was targeted a career-high nine times.

Allen said Ferguson showed he could handle the adversity that all players, especially young pass-catchers, must endure.

“It’s super hard because you’re trying to impress, but there are a lot of things you’re trying to balance,” Allen said. “You’re playing a football game, but you’re also trying to keep your job — and then there’s thousands if not millions of people watching. So you make a mistake, and it’s kind of like, ‘Ahhh.’ That’s hard to just easily brush off. It takes a true mental effort to start talking to yourself in a positive way.’”

Ferguson was happy to finish the game on a high note.

“That made it feel a little better,” he said, “scoring a touchdown.”

Broncos: RB Jonah Coleman (ankle) out; WR Marvin Mims Jr. (foot) questionable.

item.title: Letters to Sports: There's a reason the Chargers can't get untracked
item.description: Readers of the Los Angeles Times give their thoughts on the Chargers, Rams, Lakers, Dodgers and high school sports among other things.
item.content:encoded:
It’s easy to kick the Chargers while they are down, and for the Chargers to feel sorry for themselves. But the Chargers need to put their big boy pants on if they still have them.

Mario Jacques
Covina

Watch different NFL teams play. Not counting the long bomb, every team throws many passes while the receiver is running. Except the Chargers. They never throw timing passes. They never throw slants. They never throw passes before the receiver makes his breaks. Their receivers run to a spot, stop and turn around. Then Justin Herbert throws a bullet. Those plays are easy to guard and yards after the catch are low.

Plus, this year their receivers are not special and the plays they run require someone to have a lot of space when they stop. Also, with these routes, Herbert must wait longer before he throws, putting more pressure on his offensive line. No wonder they are impotent on offense.

Mike Lorraine
Simi Valley

Rams history

It was good to see the Rams celebrate their early L.A. history by wearing gold jerseys and by giving the SoFi fans 1951 championship towels. But the Rams need to do more. The only two championship banners displayed at the stadium are for their two Super Bowl wins. The franchise’s 1945 (representing Cleveland) and 1951 titles also deserve banners, similar to how the Lakers acknowledge their Minneapolis past.

The NFL existed long before the Super Bowl era, and those early championships were huge. Arguably, the 1951 championship is extra important here because it was an L.A. title, while the 1999 Super Bowl champs played in St. Louis.

Jim Bendat
Los Angeles

I have been a Rams fan for longer than almost anyone. I saw my first game in the Coliseum in 1947. (I may be a candidate for oldest Rams fan.) I have cheered for them in almost all of their games, even after they made me cry by moving to St. Louis.

But having seen them in those awful yellow uniforms, I am thinking of making a change. The Chargers have great uniforms ... maybe I should become a Chargers fan. I might even consider rooting for the long-hated 49ers, who also look pretty good in red and gray.

Russ Hoyt
Mission Viejo

Which Lake show?

Siskel and Ebert wannabes Rob Pelinka and JJ Redick of the Lakers liken themselves to iconic film protagonists. What?! As long as we’re referencing movie roles, “Dumb and Dumber” seems apt.

David Griffin
Westwood

In paying respects to LeBron James’ eight years with the Lakers, Rob Pelinka referred to his time as “an incredible era for us here.” One COVID-induced championship in eight years. Incredible?

Jack Wolf
Westwood

Keep the kid

Josue De Paula’s enthusiasm is contagious. In less than two weeks, he has turned around the entire Dodger team, transforming it from a likely first-round playoff loser to arguably a World Series favorite. Almost everyone is hitting, excitement has returned to Dodger Stadium and the organization has to keep this kid in the lineup.

Steve Wagner
Limerick, Pa.

Work of art

It was nice to see an article by Sam Farmer about Chaz Perea, landscaping manager, who is someone other than a baseball player or management at Dodger Stadium. Chaz Perea sure does have a “green thumb” working for many years with his small crew at the stadium.

If we don’t get a “three-peat,” at least Dodger fans will enjoy the botanic garden and wonderful landscaping that surrounds the stadium.

Joan C. Fingon
Ventura

End of streaks

Entering the weekend, the Angels had to win two of their last three to avoid losing 100 games for the first time in their checkered history. Similarly, without their enthusiastic owner being able to cheer in person for them (and Vegas predicting less than a 30-win season), the Clippers’ streak of 15 consecutive seasons of playing .500 or better basketball seems likely to be snapped in 2026-2027.

Ken Feldman
Tarzana

On point

Once again Eric Sondheimer has hit the nail on the head. The lack of enforcement power by the Southern Section only leads to coaches continuing to violate the rules. There is a need for a czar over all Southern Section schools with the authority to properly penalize transgressors.

Mr. Sondheimer would be great in this role though I doubt he would want it at this time. With the morals in this country at an all-time low, how can we expect high school athletes to develop into outstanding individuals when they see violators of the transfer rules receive merely a slap on the wrist?

Mark Kaiserman
Santa Monica

Rocky Top will be filled with Manning family connections on Saturday when Tennessee hosts Texas at Neyland Stadium.

The 13th-ranked Volunteers will be looking to spoil Steve Sarkisian's first trip to Knoxville as Texas' head coach and open SEC play with a statement victory over the nation's top-ranked team.

item.title: Davis Webb did exactly what he needed to do to get Broncos back on track
item.description: The regular season is already flying by it seems. We’re already heading into Week 3 and the Denver Broncos will be in prime time again — this time on Sunday Night Football to host the Los Angeles Rams. For both teams, the start to the season began with disaster and segued into a strong performance. […]
item.content:encoded:
The regular season is already flying by it seems. We’re already heading into Week 3 and the Denver Broncos will be in prime time again — this time on Sunday Night Football to host the Los Angeles Rams.

For both teams, the start to the season began with disaster and segued into a strong performance. In Denver, that first week was met with some serious meltdowns from fans over new offensive coordinator Davis Webb and him seemingly getting outplayed at every turn by Kansas City Chief defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo. In hindsight, going up against a multi-decade experienced defensive coordinator like Spags was probably not a great way to start ones career as a new offensive coordinator.

Head Coach Sean Payton was asked this week when calling plays began to feel natural to him and he sure wasn’t sure how to answer that one which makes me think maybe a coach can never get too comfortable when they are the play caller.

“There’s a learning curve, always, and then I think the most important thing is it’s not plays within the scheme, it’s players,” Payton said. “So you’re constantly moving relative to what you have. I can look at ‘06 New Orleans, I can look at ‘09, 2013, 2017 and you would be like, ‘Man, there’s some…’ But there were a lot of changes too relative to who and I think the same here or there’s some fundamental things that we want to do and yet you also move in the direction of what the skill set allows.”

It seems like he just likes to remember the good seasons when he had the most fun calling plays. I suppose that would make it feel more natural when everything is going the right way.

That answer did lead to another question about Davis Webb directly and whether or not he was evaluated unfairly after that first week.

“Yes, I think every scenario is different,” Payton said. “I think just being yourself in the process during the week and getting to the things that we think are going to fit. I think all those things go into it, but I think in each case they’re all somewhat a little different.”

And his response leads back to the whole going up against a guy like Spags in your first game as play caller. Not the ideal situation, but how Webb handled the black eye and followed it up with a stellar performance calling plays in the team’s win over the Jacksonville Jaguars is a huge check in the box for him.

Of course, at the end of the day the players executed last week and did not the previous week. As fans we can point to that, but again it would be on the coaches to have the players prepared in the first place. I personally think Webb is going to be just fine and so will the Broncos.

item.content:encoded:
Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need as the Giants get ready to take on the Tennessee Titans tomorrow at 1 p.m.

Giants’ season hinges on John Harbaugh after Jaxson Dart injury | The Athletic

We’re going to learn a lot about the New York Giants over the next few weeks. The team was delivered a gut punch with the news that second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart is out for the season with a knee injury. But coach John Harbaugh didn’t get a $100 million contract just to captain the franchise through smooth seas. This type of adversity is when Harbaugh’s talents as a culture-building coach should emerge.

Harbaugh isn’t a miracle worker. The Ravens went 6-12 in the 18 games they started a backup during the seven seasons since Lamar Jackson became their starter. The Giants don’t need a miracle, but they need Harbaugh’s leadership to prevent Dart’s injury from sending the season off the rails.

Practicing what they preach

Harbs Weekly: Turning the page to Tennessee | Giants.com

Q: Like you said, the NFL is high-level drama. With everything that has transpired this week, are you just eager to get to Sunday and turn the page?

Harbaugh: The guys are excited about the game. It’s an opportunity to get to 2-1, 1-0 for the week is the mantra. Circumstances are always what they are. So yeah, it’s a tough circumstance with the quarterback. It’s unique. We’re not the only team that’s ever faced that, not even the only team that’s facing it this week in the National Football League, and we won’t be the last team to face it. It’s not something that’s unknown to mankind. It’s an adversity that’s going to hopefully serve to make us a better football team and that’s really the goal – to become the best football team we can be. But within that, play our best football game this week and we have a team that’s really determined and really locked in to do that. Jaxson (Dart) is supporting that. He’s been in meetings all week supporting the guys and supporting Jameis (Winston). So yeah, we’re excited to play the game.

NFL Week 3 picks, predictions, schedule, odds, fantasy tips | ESPN.com

The Giants’ offense will look different against the Titans. They’ll have to cater it to QB Jameis Winston’s skill set, which doesn’t include the same running ability as Jaxson Dart (knee). The Giants already have the plays in their playbook. Guard Jon Runyan said they have more than 300 plays already. Now, OC Matt Nagy & Co. will lean on what works better for Winston. That likely means using Winston’s arm and ability to throw downfield to complement the running game.

Why are Giants barely putting Odell Beckham Jr. on the field?| New York Daily News

Beckham and Jaxson Dart never appeared to develop any obvious chemistry during training camp, but Jameis Winston and Beckham had a rapport. They’re both veterans. Winston often plants his back foot and fires, and Beckham is a precise, timing-based route runner. And Beckham logged more snaps with the backups than the starters, giving him more time on task with Winston.

And yet when Winston took over for Dart in Monday’s first quarter, and as the Giants’ offense floundered while falling behind big, Beckham was nailed to the bench. It just seems Beckham should be worked in as an option, particularly with Winston now under center.

How Giants offense changes now with Jameis Winston at quarterback | The Record

Cam Skattebo doesn’t see why anything has to change offensively for the New York Giants.

With respect and love to Jaxson Dart, whom he called “my best friend” on the day the 23-year-old was placed on injured reserve with knee surgery pending, and Jameis Winston’s ascension to a starting role, Skattebo has a solution to replacing the juice missing without Dart.

Giants trade candidate aims to spark ‘terrible’ defense: ‘It’s been hard’ | NJ.com

The Giants need their defense to lift them in Sunday’s home game against the Titans — which still seems winnable, even without quarterback Jaxson Dart.

But if coordinator Dennard Wilson’s group plays as poorly as it did Monday night in Los Angeles, the Giants are doomed — and coach John Harbaugh’s once-promising first season might begin to spiral out of control. On Sunday, they Giants will turn to a fascinating potential trade piece, outside linebacker Kayvon Thibodeaux, since elite edge rusher Brian Burns will be sidelined by an ankle sprain he sustained in that 28-6 loss to the Rams.

Special teams have been a bright spot

Giants’ young specialists giving Chris Horton something to build on | USAToday.com

Dominic Zvada supplied every Giants point in Monday night’s 28-6 loss to the Rams, hitting from 24 yards late in the first half and from 52 in the third quarter. “From the day we got him here, always believed in him, and just needed to get him out there to get him those opportunities,” Horton told reporters on Wednesday. “And we know who he is, he knows who he is. And so, it was very encouraging to get him out there in a game setting and let him kick that 52-yard field goal.”

Jordan Stout is the other half of that battery. Horton said the punter’s ability to flip the field has been outstanding, including 70-plus-yard boots and one that approached 80. That only works if the rest of the unit lets it work. “You can’t allow him to do the things that he does if you don’t allow your punt coverage, also those other guys to work,” Horton said. “Situationally, we’re just allowing him to be who he is, and it just starts with everybody understanding what kind of punter we have. We protect the punt, and then we need all-out effort. That’s from all the other 10 guys.”

item.title: Orlando Brown Jr. believes the 2026 Bengals are a Super Bowl team
item.description: The Bengals left tackle has a Super Bowl ring of his own
item.content:encoded:
The expectations and pressure were at an all-time high for the Cincinnati Bengals entering the 2026 season after missing the playoffs for three straight years.

Although it is still incredibly early, the Bengals’ revamped roster has shown up and executed at a winning level.

The Bengals are 2-0 with a healthy Joe Burrow for the first time in the Zac Taylor era, and the defense has been lights out through the first two weeks.

One of the biggest reasons for the early success is the new additions on the defensive side that are not only veterans but also Super Bowl champions.

The front office brought in Boye Mafe and Bryan Cook, two guys that have won Super Bowls at their previous stops in the NFL.

The Bengals also have another guy on the roster who has Super Bowl experience as well, and that is left tackle Orlando Brown Jr.

Brown recently had an interview with Casino.org and shared that he believes this is a Super Bowl-caliber roster and a roster that is even better than the one he was a part of on the Chiefs.

“To be honest, this is nothing like I’ve ever been a part of,” Brown said. “We are very unique in so many different ways when I look at our offense, defense, and special teams units. I’ve never been a part of anything like this.”

As I said earlier in the article, the expectations are at an all-time high this season, and it is clear the players on the roster feel the exact same way.

item.title: A 63-point plunge in fan confidence and a split on Jayden Daniels’ season - survey results
item.description: Fans move past single-game anger to debate Adam Peters' draft hit rates, veteran trades, and the rebuild recalibration timeline.
item.content:encoded:
Most weeks of the year, and every week of the season for several years now, Hogs Haven runs Reacts surveys, and I write an article breaking down the results. Because I’m writing about what Hogs Haven readers have said in a collective sense, I rely heavily on the comments section to inform what I write. The collective opinion expressed in the survey may not always match my own, but I try to offer an honest peek into the reasons behind the numbers as best I can make sense of them.

This week, I want to take a slightly different approach to analyzing the survey results, as you’ll see in the article below.

This week, we asked two questions, which is our norm during the regular season.

Question 1: Fan confidence

The first question asked, as it does every week of the season (at least until early December), whether you are confident in the team’s direction.

From our first survey to our second—before and after the opener in Philadelphia—confidence actually climbed from 70% to 83%. That early surge seemed based entirely on the “quality” of the loss: Washington went on the road against an elite Eagles team, pushed them to the brink in a 24-22 nail-biter, and looked competitive throughout. The general feeling was that the outcome turned on a handful of fixable execution errors.

This week, however, confidence collapsed to just 20%.

A 37-20 loss in Dallas will do that to a fan base. The defense looked disjointed, the secondary surrendered big plays through the air, and the interior offensive line struggled in short-yardage spots. To make matters worse, franchise quarterback Jayden Daniels suffered another dislocation to his left elbow on the final play of the first half.

Sitting at 0-2 overall and 0-2 in the NFC East with the Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks arriving in Landover for the home opener, fans are not, to put it mildly, feeling optimistic.

Question 2: Jayden Daniels’ 2026 outlook

The second question in our survey asked whether you believe Jayden Daniels’ 2026 season came to an end with his injury in Dallas.

Visit our partners at FanDuel

In a roughly 60:40 split, the majority of survey respondents — who voted in the poll before any update or decision was announced by the team — believed that Jayden would return to the field at some point this season.

Again, voting took place early in the week before we had much official word from the team. On Friday, GM Adam Peters gave an update on his weekly radio appearance, and later in the day, head coach Dan Quinn provided confirmation on Daniels’ status.

It turns out that the 59% of fans who expected Jayden to return this season were right, at least, according to both AP and DQ, though the exact timing of his return remains up in the air aside from the fact that he is not being placed on IR at the moment.

The significance of not being put on injured reserve

As you are probably aware, players who are on IR must miss at least 4 games. For Daniels, a stint on IR would have meant Weeks 3 to 6, followed by a bye in Week 7, with a return allowed no earlier than Week 8 at home against the Eagles.

The fact that he is not being put on IR signals that the team expects him to return to play earlier, meaning in Week 4, 5 or 6, against the Colts in London, Giants in Landover, or the 49ers in San Francisco.

The Noah Brown lesson

Of course, we all remember WR Noah Brown, who, last season, was injured in the Week 2 game vs the Packers. He was not immediately placed on IR, indicating that the team expected him to return by the Week 6 game in mid-October. Instead, when that mid-October date arrived, Brown was not activated, instead being put on IR on October 15th and staying there until early December.

So, while it is clear that Adam Peters, Dan Quinn and Jayden himself all expect or hope for his return to play sometime in October, the example of Noah Brown from last season reminds us that return from injury is an uncertain process.

In any event, one thing is clear — the team, like the majority of our survey respondents — expect Jayden to be back as captain and quarterback in the coming weeks.

Commanders fans: Make your pick in the SB Nation app!

Take Reacts surveys, create Commanders polls, and see how your answers compare with fellow Hogs Haven fans. Then discuss the results with the Burgundy and Gold community.

Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android.

An experiment: Mapping 740+ comments with AI

As I noted at the top, I try to integrate the thoughts of survey respondents into these weekly articles. This week, I faced both a challenge and an interesting opportunity.

The survey article generated over 210 comments on Tuesday and Wednesday. Meanwhile, Monday’s All aTwitter post had drawn more than 530 comments following the Dallas game and covering much of the same territory. Across just 72 hours, this community posted roughly three-quarters of a million words dissecting the state of the franchise in the context of Daniels’ (re)injury.

Rather than cherry-picking 4 or 5 comments and calling it a day, I decided to try something different. Having read so much about how Artificial Intelligence is revolutionizing work flows around the world, I figured I could ‘opt in’ and make the revolution work for me. I fed all 530+ comments from Monday’s All aTwitter and all 210+ comments from the Reacts thread into Gemini, asking it to summarize the arguments and track how community sentiment evolved as the week progressed.

I know there is plenty of justifiable skepticism across the internet about AI content replacing human writers. Rest assured, I am not handing over my keyboard, but as an analytical tool for mapping community psychology, it seemed like the perfect opportunity to integrate some of the latest technology into my decidedly low-tech writing.

What follows in the italicized block below is the AI-generated synthesis of your comments across both threads:

The community breakdown (generated via Comment Text Analysis)

1. Immediate aftermath: The Monday vent (All aTwitter)

Following the Dallas game, comments reflected acute shock, in-game tactical frustration, and heated debate over Daniels:

  • The Daniels status debate: Discussion split between a minority urging Daniels to get fitted with a brace and return immediately to protect his developmental momentum (LionRoars1987 citing Kurt Warner) and a strong majority rejecting that path, citing re-injury risk and pain. Debate also sparked over whether awkwardly planting an arm is a recurring durability issue or an unavoidable fluke.
  • In-game frustrations: Sharp criticism focused on end-of-half clock management—specifically Daniels trying to make a play rather than taking an easy field goal—leaving the team down 7 rather than 4. Commenters tallied missed opportunities and called out interior offensive line failures in short-yardage spots under center.
  • Front office & staff: Sweeping criticism emerged regarding GM Adam Peters’ three-year roster build, pointing to depth issues along the offensive line and in the secondary. Commenters vented about Dan Quinn’s game management, with a few floating early speculation about offensive coordinator David Blough.

2. Midweek realism: The Reacts survey thread

By Tuesday and Wednesday, comments shifted from raw emotional venting to a structured, polarized audit of the rebuild:

  • Orthopedic Consensus vs. Long-Term Health: Discussion matured into medical analysis, citing Tommy John timelines and joint stability. A significant contingent argued for shutting Daniels down for season-ending corrective surgery to safeguard his future rather than rushing him back in a brace to chase an 0-2 season. Durability concerns grew more explicit regarding his frame and fall mechanics.
  • On GM Adam Peters: A deep ideological divide emerged. Poster Rook6980 mounted a multi-paragraph, probabilistic defense of Adam Peters, pointing out the barren baseline left by Ron Rivera and calculating the mathematical reality of turning over 20+ starters. Skeptics pushed back, arguing three offseasons should yield better depth, with a few radical commenters proposing a total fire-sale of older assets (Terry McLaurin, Laremy Tunsil, Daron Payne) to bottom out for high draft picks.
  • Coaching accountability: Skepticism around Dan Quinn hardened, with posters pointing to historical trends and staff cohesion, balanced against older fans expressing “rebuild fatigue” over the prospect of another coaching reset.

3. The 48-hour transition

The progression from Monday to Wednesday tracked a clear shift from acute trauma to structural diagnosis:

  • From panic to medicine: Daniels discourse shifted from in-game blame to long-term orthopedic preservation.
  • From venting to roster economics: Frustration moved from single-game blown plays to deep debates over draft hit rates and multi-year rebuild baselines.
  • From shared agony to in-fighting: The collective commiseration of Monday gave way to internal friction midweek over unverified injury leaks and community pessimism.

Perspective: Separating the pain from the process

Reading that Gemini-generated synthesis confirms what many of us felt all week: when a season starts 0-2 and the franchise quarterback gets hurt, emotional balance sheets quickly run into the red. But stepping back from the immediate pain of what happened in the Dallas game allows for a less emotional look at where the team stands. Let’s take a look at the key thematic outcomes of those quarter-million words:

  • On the Daniels Decision: Comments from fans show that they believe that if surgical stabilization were required to protect Daniels’ non-throwing elbow for the next decade (and apparently he believes, after consultation with doctors that it isn’t), he would need to be shut down without hesitation. The team should not risk a chronic, career-altering joint issue behind a transitional offensive line to salvage a handful of wins in a retooling year. At the same time, fans point out that everyone should avoid seeing an awkward fall on the field and labeling a young passer “brittle.” Dislocating an elbow while trying to maintain footing is a freakish event that does not signal an inability to handle the NFL game.
  • On the Rebuild Timeline: The debate between posters like Rook6980 and the Peters skeptics gets to the heart of roster-building economics. When Adam Peters took over, this roster was effectively devoid of cheap, drafted starter depth. Rebuilding an entire two-deep roster through the draft takes three to four full cycles. Tearing it down further by trading anchors like McLaurin, Tunsil, or Payne accomplishes little except accelerating dead money onto the cap and stripping away the protection Daniels needs when he is healthy.
  • On Coaching Stability: Washington lived on the three-year coaching carousel for more than a quarter of a century. Dan Quinn and his defensive staff face legitimate schematic questions after two rough divisional outings, but calling for staff overhauls two games into the season merely guarantees another multi-year identity reset.

National sentiment

In addition to our blog-based survey, SB Nation also sends out email surveys to those who register to participate.

In this week’s national survey, fans of all 32 teams were asked to identify which 0-2 team is most likely to make the playoffs. Without Jayden Daniels to lean on, sentiment for the Commanders was extremely muted.

Visit our partners at FanDuel

Fans across the league were also asked which one, in the rash of recent quarterback injuries, would hurt his team’s playoff chances the most. I’m, frankly, a bit surprised that 31% of fans nationally thought that Washington had any playoff chances to hurt.

Looking ahead to Week 3

We all know that the schedule maker didn’t do Washington any favors in the first quarter of the 2026 season (though there is relief in the second half). After opening with two division games on the road, when Washington finally comes back to Landover for the season home opener, they face the defending champion Seattle Seahawks at Northwest Stadium on Sunday. Unsurprisingly, FanDuel currently lists Seattle as heavy road favorites.

  • Point Spread: Seattle -7
  • Game Total (Over/Under): 40.5 points

With Marcus Mariota getting the nod under center, Sunday’s home opener is an early gut check for the Commanders. The fan base is understandably bruised, but seasons turn on how organizations weather turbulent stretches. This is another opportunity for a re-made roster and coaching staff to show that they won’t be defined by a couple of road losses and some bad injury luck.

Kickoff against the Seahawks is at 1:00 PM on Sunday. Buckle up. It should be an eventful afternoon!

item.title: Saquon Barkley explains why he returned vs. Titans after scary neck injury
item.description: Saquon Barkley called his neck injury a wake-up call but expects to play Monday night against the Bears.
item.content:encoded:
Saquon Barkley explains why he returned vs. Titans after scary neck injury originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

If you were shocked to see Saquon Barkley return to the field Sunday after suffering a serious-looking neck injury in the first half of the Eagles-Titans game, you’re not alone.

“I know it made a lot of people upset,” Barkley said Friday at his locker. 

Barkley suffered a stinger – a nerve injury in his neck – on the first play of the game, which the Eagles went on to win 24-20. It’s not an injury players generally return from in the same game, but Barkley played 11 snaps in the second half and carried the ball three times for nine yards.

“I talked to (the trainers and doctors) and they allowed me,” he said. “I was honest with them. I said if I feel something again I’ll come out. I tried my best to go back out there. It didn’t go the way I thought it was going to go. But looking back on it, I wouldn’t change anything.

“We’re competitors. I waited and let it calm down. At first, I didn’t have my strength. I felt like I got my strength back. And they put me in position to allow me to go out there after I kind of begged for it. But I also told them at the same time that I’m gonna protect myself. If I feel something, you got my word. 

“I want to be out there and competing for my team. Sadly, it didn’t go the way I would like it. But, you know, got a chance to go back out there this week.”

Barkley underwent an MRI on Monday to see exactly what was going on in his neck. He said he’s had numerous previous stingers of varying degrees of seriousness and called this one of the worst he’s had.

“Nerve things are scary,” he said. “It’s not the first stinger I ever got. It won’t be the last. But some are worse than others. … “Some hurt a little more than others. I won’t go into detail about it, but some just hurt a little more than others. Sometimes you get it, you guys won’t even know.

“That was really the big thing with MRI, making sure I didn’t really do anything crazy and anything worse. I’ve had a history of it before, just the first bad one I had in a long time. It’s kind of like in football, your neck can get put in certain ways. But also like a wake-up call to me. I’ve been very super focused on like my lower body and my longevity in my career. Probably wasn’t as great as I needed to be with my neck stability and strengthening in my neck. 

“So it’s like just putting that within my routine and having that part of my process and kind the same way I attack everything from head to toe, do the same thing with my neck and go out there. 

“It’s good to have the MRI knowing that’s nothing, hopefully, God willing, about my career. And I can just go out there and play free and try to get, don’t want to say get this thing going because we’re 2-0, just keep it rolling. There’s obviously some things we want to improve on in the offense, especially in the run game. I’m ready for the opportunity to keep attacking that.”

The Eagles listed Barkley as limited at practice on Thursday, but he was a full participant on Friday and said he expects to play Monday night in the Eagles’ nationally televised prime-time game against the Bears at Soldier Field.

He said he’ll be wearing a collar but said it won’t limit how he can turn his head like the one he wore when he returned to the field for the second half against the Titans.

“When I first put it on, I really couldn’t turn my head,” he said. “I was trying to tell them that your head is like your steering wheel for me to run. So when I went out there, I actually tried to get into a running back stance, and I was like stuck. I had to try to change my stance. So my stance might look a little different.

“But the (equipment staff) did a really good job of coming up with something that is not only going to protect me but also allow me to play the way I want to play and play free.”

It has been an un-Saquon-esque start to the season. He did have a 42-yard run in the opener, but more than half of his carries so far – 10 of 19 – have gone for three yards or less. 

The 42-yarder is the only run by an Eagles running back this year over 10 yards.

“My strength is back,” Barkley said after practice Friday. “We’re calming the nerve down. And I’m blessed I get to play Monday night against the Chicago Bears. And I’m excited for that.”

item.title: The thing that has to change for Eagles defense without pressing
item.description: The Eagles haven't gotten a takeaway in two games. That's something that needs to change going forward.
item.content:encoded:
The thing that has to change for Eagles defense without pressing originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio earlier this week summed up one of the biggest issues with the 2026 Eagles defense so far with just two words.

“We’re due,” Fangio said.

They don’t have a single takeaway yet.

It might not sound like a big deal because it has only been two games. But the Eagles are one of just three teams in the NFL without a takeaway through two weeks and the others — the Texans and Commanders — are both 0-2.

The Eagles are 2-0 and it’s hard to get there without forcing a turnover. In fact, the Eagles are just the fifth team in NFL history to begin a season with a 2-0 record despite not having a takeaway, joining the 1984 49ers, 1998 Broncos, 2016 Giants and 2025 Buccaneers.

So the Eagles need to start getting some takeaways. But they have to do it within the flow of the game. They can’t force it.

“We have to tackle and not miss tackles because we’re trying to go for the ball,” Fangio said. “That bugs me.”

“Sometimes those come in bunches,” said head coach Nick Sirianni, who has always stressed the importance of turnover differential. “We work like crazy on it. I wouldn’t say that we’ve had a ball that I felt like we dropped as far as an interception goes. We’ve had a couple scrambles against quarterbacks that are good at getting out of the pocket with our first two opponents. You haven’t had a couple of those strip-sack fumbles that you get sometimes in those scenarios.

“You get more tackling attempts than you do takeaway attempts in a game. So, your tackling fundamentals come first, always. You don’t want to put the tackle at risk by going after a strip-attempt. We chart this every week: ‘Hey, here’s how many strip attempt opportunities there were. Here’s how many times we took an attempt at it.’ You can’t score points unless you shoot the ball. Those are judged by us as far as when we tell them to take these strip attempts, but you never sacrifice the tackle in any case.”

That’s a fine line to walk. The Eagles want to make the most of their opportunities but don’t want to force it. Because there’s a difference between being aggressive and being reckless.

“If you want to do too much,” Jordan Davis said, “then you probably end up doing nothing.”

Sirianni on Thursday gave credit to the Commanders and Titans for having good ball security.

And, for the most part, the Eagles haven’t really had many chances to take the ball away. It’s not like they have been dropping interceptions or missing loose balls. There have been just a handful of opportunities through two games.

In Week 1, Jalen Carter punched out a ball in the fourth quarter that was recovered by the Commanders. In Week 2, Jihaad Campbell forced a fumble that went out of bounds and Riq Woolen had one ball that was fired just behind him that he couldn’t corral for a pick.

Woolen, 27, had 12 interceptions in his first four NFL seasons, so he’s known for his ballhawk ability. Woolen said it’s part effort and part skill. He admitted this week it can get “a little bit” frustrating when those takeaways aren’t coming.

“But at the same time,we keep getting turnovers on downs, so that’s good,” Woolen said. “But being able to get a takeaway, it electrifies the team and it boosts confidence throughout the team. It’s going to come. It’s going to come with the playing style. All of us play hard. If we play one snap at a time, one of those snaps is going to be a takeaway. And when it happens, we’re going to be celebrating.”

The Eagles last season were slightly above average in takeaways. They had 21 in 17 games, which ranked tied for 10th in the NFL. In 2025, the Eagles had just three games without a takeaway and they were 1-2 in those games. 

Through two games, the Eagles’ defense hasn’t been elite but it still has that potential. And a few takeaways would go a long way to helping them get there.

It’s always going to be a focus.

“We drill it unlike anybody at the end of the day, and we talk about it,” Sirianni said. “We’ve just got to stick to the process, and I think that’s such a key. Can you stick to the process when you’re not producing results? Can you stick to what you know is going to get the ball out when the results aren’t there yet? That’s a key in not just takeaways, but everything. Can you stick to that thing knowing that the work’s going to be what gets the ball out when you have those opportunities in the game?”

item.title: Bud Light creates eye-popping ‘Celly Jar’ winnings for Kyle Juszczyk ‘drinking’ fine
item.description: Bud Light, the NFL’s official drinking sponsor, is looking to take advantage of every marketing opportunity it can get. The beer company is opening a “Celly Jar” that will reward...
item.content:encoded:
Bud Light, the NFL’s official drinking sponsor, is looking to take advantage of every marketing opportunity it can get.

The beer company is opening a “Celly Jar” that will reward fans with $37,384 to celebrate.

“It’s been a busy week of beer and celebrations! And Bud Light, the Official Beer Sponsor of the NFL, loves to celebrate responsibly,” the company wrote in an email that was released by NFL insider Ari Meirov. “… Why $37,384? Seemed like a fine amount.”

The email ends with the company telling fans to “keep an eye on Bud Light social media channels this weekend to learn how they can receive $10 off a single purchase of Bud Light (12-pack or larger) to celebrate responsibly.”

The total number of the “Celly Jar” adds up to the same amount that the NFL fined 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk, Colts guard Matt Goncalves and Cowboys tight end Jake Ferguson for having drinking celebrations last week.

Juszczyk was given the highest fine among the three at $14,926. Ferguson was billed $13,611, and Goncalves was charged $8,847.

The three of them have appealed the fines.

Juszczyk said he wasn’t pretending to drink alcohol, and even added that he does not drink it.

The 49ers fullback said his celebration is an ode to his nickname on the field, “Juice,” and also added that when he receives the ball during the game, you can hear fans in the stadium chant, “Juiiccceee.”

Despite the fine being an inconvenience, Juszczyk has been getting the most attention, and he’s been having fun with it.

The trolling of his fine first began after his longtime friend and teammate George Kittle hopped in on the fun by posting a photo of Juszczyk on his X account and told the NFL, “This guy is a menace.”

After the 49ers concluded practice on Thursday, Juszczyk taped over a bottle in his locker and made a makeshift label that read “NOT BEER” and also had a graphic of a juice box, with his No. 44 on it.

When he got home, he and his wife, Kristin Juszczyk, had one last joke before the day came to an end by creating a TikTok video of them making homemade juice, where they were both seen aggressively cutting oranges and squeezing the juice out of them.

item.title: Jaguars vs. Patriots predictions: Brenton Strange is due
item.description: Could this be the week the Jaguars get Strange activated in the pass game?
item.content:encoded:
The Jacksonville Jaguars (1-1) are back at EverBank Stadium to face the New England Patriots (1-1) in Week 3. The teams last met in Week 7 of the 2024 season, when Tank Bigsby rushed for a career-high 118 yards and 2 touchdowns in a 34-16 Jags win at Wembley Stadium.

According to FanDuel Sportsbook, the Jaguars are 2.5-point favorites against the Patriots this week. Home-field advantage is generally worth a 3-point swing, so on a neutral field, Jacksonville would be 0.5-point underdogs. I have a feeling that’s the mentality the team will be operating with anyway after last week’s narrow loss at Mile High.

Let’s get to some predictions.

Prediction #1

Did you know that the Jaguars were 11-1 last season when Brenton Strange played? He was a pillar of Liam Coen’s offense, and Jacksonville secured him on a long-term extension in the offseason.

Though two games this year, Strange only has 4 catches (5 targets) for 40 yards and 1 touchdown.

Total.

There may be “a lot of mouths to feed” between Parker Washington and Brian Thomas Jr. and Jakobi Meyers in the wide receiver room, but Trevor Lawrence already has 52 pass attempts. That equates to a 9.6% target share for Strange so far. When healthy last season, he had a 16% target share.

Good news: this underwhelming box-score start is nothing to fret about. Strange is due for work in the passing game, and not just because of natural regression after a small sample of games. He ran crisp routes against the Broncos in Week 2, but for various reasons, Lawrence wasn’t looking his way a few times when he popped wide open.

I think the team could see that on tape and say, “Oh, yeah. We just paid this guy because we think he’s really good. Maybe we should try to get him the ball more often.”

If/when New England’s interior pass rush disrupts Lawrence on Sunday, it’ll be even more of a reason to lean into short-area passing concepts featuring Strange.

The prediction: Brenton Strange matches his current 2026 receiving stats

Strange has +300 odds on FanDuel to score a touchdown, and his receiving yardage over/under line is set at 27.5 yards.

Prediction #2

Jacksonville’s run defense has merely been above average this season after being the league’s best in 2025. The fact that the Broncos ran free for 1st downs to clinch last week’s game was alarming, to say the least.

Expect the Jaguars to tighten up against a Patriots offense that wants to run the ball but isn’t all that threatening when it does. While Rhamondre Stevenson is among the most underappreciated rushers in football, he’s a jack-of-all-trades with no elite traits and a real issue holding onto the rock. And while 2025 second-round pick TreVeyon Henderson is among the most explosive rushers in football, he requires a wide-open rushing lane to inflict maximum damage. How valuable is a slugger if he can only connect on fastballs down the middle?

New England’s running back room is solid yet unremarkable. Their starting offensive line looked promising to start the season, but right guard Mike Onwenu fractured his ankle in Week 2.

Jacksonville ought to shut down the opposing running game, the same way they did so many times last season, but the real question is whether they can contain a dual-threat quarterback. Can the Jags prevent out-of-structure playmaking from last year’s MVP runner-up?

The prediction: Drake Maye leads the Patriots in rushing yards

On FanDuel, Maye’s rushing yards over/under line is set at 26.5 yards. Stevenson’s line is at 37.5 yards; Henderson’s line is at 41.5 yards.

Prediction #3

Josh Hines-Allen has played 112 NFL games (including playoffs). Last week’s loss in Denver was just his seventh career game without recording a pressure.

According to NFL Pro, Hines-Allen has a career-low 9.3% so far this season. He recorded a double-digit pressure rate in each of his seven prior seasons.

Jacksonville’s pass rush was already a concern going into this season, mostly because of the apparent lack of depth behind Hines-Allen and Travon Walker. If Hines-Allen isn’t playing like a No. 1 guy, the Jags could be screwed!

Fortunately, like Strange, I expect Hines-Allen to bounce back. It feels like we do this every season — he goes through a dry spell, then fans scapegoat him for a holistic roster issue, then he eventually re-finds his dominance.

After posting a Tony Snell stat line against All-Pro left tackle Garrett Bowles, Hines-Allen has a great opportunity to turn his season around on Sunday against Will Campbell.

The Patriots’ 2025 first-round pick probably isn’t as bad as he’s publicly perceived after a rocky rookie postseason — and his stats this year are actually pretty solid — but at the end of the day, Campbell should have trouble handling Hines-Allen one-on-one. The former has T-Rex arms and a poor anchor. The latter tends to feast against inferior competition.

Remember those “Have a Day!” social media graphics the NFL used to post? If they were still doing that, I’d bet Hines-Allen would have one after playing the Patriots.

The prediction: Josh Hines-Allen records a sack, a tipped pass, and a turnover

item.title: After Week 2 stinger, Saquon Barkley vows to be "fearless"
item.description: Barkley missed much of Sunday's game after injury.
item.content:encoded:
A stinger grossly shortened Eagles running back Saquon Barkley's day against the Titans in Week 2. As a Week 3 Monday night game against the Bears looms, Barkley is undeterred — but also cognizant of the situation.

"I’ve had a history of [stingers] before," Barkley said Friday, via Tim McManus of ESPN. "This is the first bad one I had in a long time. It's also like a wake-up call to me. I've been super active focusing on my lower body and longevity of my career. I probably wasn't as great as I needed to be with my neck stability and strengthening my neck. So it's putting that within my routine and having that as part of my process and kind of the same way I attack everything from head to toe, do the same thing with my neck.

"It's good to have an MRI knowing it's nothing, hopefully, God willing, where I worry about my career and I can just go out there and play free."

The injury happened on the first play from scrimmage at Tennessee. Barkley later returned wearing a neck collar, but he finished the day with only four carries for nine yards and one catch for 11 yards.

Barkley was limited in practice on Thursday. He fully participated on Friday.

Will the injury affect him on Monday?

"I don't think so," Barkley said. "That's why I'm rehabbing my ass off, to get it as strong as it needs to be. I feel like I'm in a really good spot. I know they wouldn't let me go out there if I wasn't able to do it.

"I'm going to let the game come, and I'm going to go out there and play fearless, don't worry about."

The Eagles are 2-0 after narrow wins against the overmatched Commanders and Titans. Philly may be facing a third-string quarterback in Chicago on Monday night, giving the Eagles a golden opportunity to move to 3-0.

item.title: Rams vs. Broncos predictions: Will SNF be a defensive slugfest?
item.description: Despite Sean McVay and Sean Payton being offensive minds, Sunday Night Football could be a defensive battle
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams will travel to Mile High Stadium to face the Denver Broncos on Sunday Night Football. So that means it’s time for another round of bold predictions! Last week, I hit on 1 of 5 predictions; Matthew Stafford’s four touchdown passes being the winning prediction. I had predicted that Puka Nacua would go for 175+ yards but he was inactive and Davante Adams picked up that yardage and then some.

Los Angeles enters the matchup as 2.5-point favorites, according to FanDuel. With the cross conference matchup expected to be a Super Bowl preview, here are my bold predictions for Week 3.

1. Neither defense records a sack

Both defenses are in the top half of the league, but both offensive lines are considered top 10 in the NFL. The Rams have only allowed 1 sack this year.

On the flip side, the Broncos have two of the league’s best offensive linemen in Garrett Bolles and Quinn Meinerz. Sean Payton will also be determined to make sure that Aaron Donald does not wreck his gameplan.

2. Blake Corum outrushes Kyren Williams

Last week both running backs carried the ball 12 times. KW was the leading rusher but not by much. Corum’s tape showed a runner that had the ability to hit running lanes and show acceleration and burst. I think Corum will be pushing Williams for more playing time here soon.

3. Score tied 13-13 entering 4th quarter

Through 3 quarters, the Broncos and Rams will be tied at 13 apiece; setting up a nail biting fourth quarter. I think the team that finds the second touchdown first will ultimately prevail.

4. Tutu Atwell catches 3 passes

Just when you wonder how/why Tutu Atwell is on the Rams roster, he finds a way to make himself useful on the game field. With the need to stretch the defense and test some of the cornerbacks on the outside, Tutu becomes a useful gadget; hauling in 3 passes for 58 yards.

5. Rams offense converts two fourth down calls

In an attempt to kickstart the offense, the Rams go for it on 4th down not once but twice. They convert both times; resulting in both drives getting points.

item.title: Raiders’ Klint Kubiak makes an eye popping observation for matchup against Saints
item.description: While the Las Vegas Raiders have been one of the more impressive teams through the first two weeks of the season, the New Orleans Saints have been just as impressive — which could allude to a potential problem for the Raiders.
item.content:encoded:
While the Las Vegas Raiders have been one of the more impressive teams through the first two weeks of the season, the New Orleans Saints have been just as impressive — which could allude to a potential problem for the Raiders.

The noise of the Caesars Superdome.

After the Raiders concluded their final practice for the week, before they travel to New Orleans, Kubiak talked about the struggles of playing in the Superdome as an opponent on the road.

“You can prep them as much as you want, but once you get there to an environment like that, it’s a whole new ballgame,” Kubiak said. “It’s a great environment to play.”

Both the Raiders and Saints have a lot more to smile about these days than they have in the past four seasons.

The Raiders are off to a 2-0 start for the first time since 2021. The Saints are coming off an impressive 24-17 victory against the Baltimore Ravens. As well as a near-overtime victory against the Detroit Lions in Week 1.

A large part of the Saints’ success is owed to second-year head coach Kellen Moore and quarterback Tyler Shough.

Shough has thrown for 662 yards with four touchdowns and two interceptions in the early stages of the season.
